# Google

This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the **public domain**. A <term>public domain<note>A status belonging to creative works upon which no intellectual property rights—such as copyright—apply, usually because the rights have expired or were forfeited.</note></term> book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <margin>marginalia</margin> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

*   **Make non-commercial use of the files** We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.
*   **Refrain from automated querying** Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, <term>optical character recognition<note>Often abbreviated as OCR; the electronic conversion of images of typed, handwritten or printed text into machine-encoded text.</note></term>, or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.
*   **Maintain attribution** The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.
*   **Keep it legal** Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## About Google Book Search

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. You can search through the full text of this book on the web at http://books.google.com/

# HEINRICH
## CORNELIUS AGRIPPA
### OF NETTESHEIM, COUNSELOR AND ARCHIVIST <note>original: "a' consiliis et archivis inditiarii"</note> TO THE SACRED <term>IMPERIAL MAJESTY<note>Agrippa served as a counselor and historian to the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V.</note></term>.

->## THREE BOOKS ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.<-

[Woodcut device showing hands holding chains connected to a ring with the text "IN GOOD FAITH <note>original: "BONA FIDE"</note>."]

->LYON,<-
->At the house of Godefroy and Marcel<-
->Bering, brothers,<-
->1550.<-

<summary>This is the title page for the 1550 edition of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's seminal work on Renaissance magic and philosophy, "De Occulta Philosophia." It identifies Agrippa's high-ranking status as an advisor and archivist to the Holy Roman Emperor.</summary>

--- Page 3 ---
<meta>This page follows the title page of the 1550 Lyon edition. It is the author's preface, "Ad Lectorem" (To the Reader), where Agrippa defends his work against potential accusations of heresy or black magic by defining the true, "noble" nature of magic as a pursuit of wisdom.</meta>

# TO THE READER.

**[Woodcut Initial N]** **I DO NOT DOUBT** that the title of our book on **Occult Philosophy**, or on **Magic**, will by its very rarity entice many to read it. Among these, some of a weak mind and biased opinion, and many also who are malicious and ungrateful toward our talent, will approach. In their reckless ignorance, these people—taking the name of **Magic** in its worst sense—will, having hardly seen the title, cry out that we teach forbidden arts, scatter the seeds of heresy, and are an offense to pious ears and a scandal to noble minds. They will cry out that I am an evildoer, a superstitious man, and a demoniac <note>original: "demoniacum," meaning one possessed by or working with demons</note>, simply because I am a magician.

To these people, I would respond that among learned men, the word **magician** does not signify an evildoer, a superstitious person, or a demoniac. Instead, it signifies a wise man, a priest, and a prophet. The <term>Sibyls<note>Prophetic women of the ancient world whose oracles were later interpreted by Christians as foretelling the coming of Jesus.</note></term> were magicians, and thus they prophesied most clearly concerning Christ. Furthermore, the <term>Magi<note>The "Three Wise Men" from the East. Agrippa uses them as a primary example to prove that magic can be holy and directed toward God.</note></term> recognized that Christ, the author of the world himself, was born by observing the wondrous secrets of the world, and they were the first of all to come to adore him. Thus, the name of **Magic** is accepted by philosophers, praised by theologians, and is not even unwelcome to the Gospel itself. 

I believe those censors of such stubborn arrogance would sooner banish the Sibyls, the holy Magi, and even the Gospel itself, than they would receive the name of magic into their favor. They are so carefully guarding their own conscience that neither Apollo, nor all the Muses, nor even an angel from heaven could save me from their curse. 

To those people, I now give this advice: do not read our writings, do not try to understand them, and do not remember them. For they are harmful; they are poisonous. The <term>Gate of Acheron<note>original: "Acherontis ostium." Acheron was a river in the Greek underworld; Agrippa is warning that for the narrow-minded, this book is a doorway to hell or destruction.</note></term> is in this book; it "speaks stones" <note>An idiom meaning the text is harsh, difficult, or potentially injurious to the unprepared.</note>—let them beware lest it dash out their brains. 

But for you who come to read with an open mind, if you use as much discretion and wisdom as bees do when gathering honey, then read in safety. For I think you will receive no small amount of benefit and a great deal of pleasure. But if you find anything that does not please you, set it aside and do not use it; for I do not endorse those things to you, but merely recount them <note>Agrippa frequently uses this legalistic defense: he is "reporting" ancient opinions rather than "affirming" them as his own beliefs.</note>. Yet do not reject the rest of the work for that reason. For it even happens that those looking into the volumes of physicians read of poisons alongside the antidotes and medicines. I confess, moreover, that magic itself contains many superfluous things,

--- Page 4 ---
<meta>This page continues Agrippa’s "To the Reader" preface. He is addressing potential critics by explaining that while some "magic" is vain, the magic he describes is for the benefit of humanity and the preservation of health and honor. He also provides the publishing history of the manuscript, explaining why a work he once "retracted" is now being printed.</meta>

...to teach curious wonders, and at the same time to ignore these as vain arts. But those things which belong to the benefit of men, to averting bad outcomes, to destroying sorceries, to curing <unclear>damaged</unclear> diseases, to exterminating phantoms, and to preserving the dexterity of life, honor, and fortune, without offense to God and without injury to religion: who would judge those not as useful as they are also necessary? 

But because I have warned you that I have written everything by narrating rather than by affirming—for so it seemed best, so that we might pass over fewer things—we have furthermore followed many opinions of the **Platonists** and other pagan philosophers where they suggested an argument for our purpose of writing. Therefore, if there is any error anywhere, or if anything is said too freely, forgive our youth; for I composed this work when I was younger than an adolescent <note>Agrippa likely wrote the first draft of this work around 1509-1510, when he was approximately 23 years old.</note>, so that I might excuse myself and say: *When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things* <note>Agrippa is quoting the Apostle Paul from 1 Corinthians 13:11 to justify his early interest in magic.</note>. 

And in our book on the *Vanity and Uncertainty of the Sciences*, I have retracted this book in large part. But here you will perhaps rebuke me again, saying: "Behold, you wrote as a youth, and retracted as an old man; why then did you publish it?" I confess I began writing these books when quite young, yet hoping to release them later more corrected and enriched; for that reason, I first offered them to be corrected by **Johannes Trithemius** <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a famous Benedictine abbot, polymath, and cryptographer who acted as a mentor to Agrippa.</note>, Abbot of Peapolis (formerly of Sponheim), a man most industrious in secret matters. 

But it happened afterward that the work was intercepted before I had put the finishing touch to it. Because the copies were corrupted, it was circulated as a truncated and unpolished work, and it flew through many hands in Italy, France, and Germany. And now some people, more impatiently—or perhaps more impudently—wished to subject this unformed work to the printing press. Struck by this one evil, I decided to publish it myself, thinking there would be less danger if these books came forth from my own hand a bit more refined than if they were made public through the hands of others as mangled and disordered fragments. 

Besides, I thought it no sin if I did not allow a specimen of my youth to perish. Moreover, we have added some chapters and inserted many things which it seemed careless to omit, which a curious reader will easily detect from the unevenness of the phrasing itself; for we did not wish to renew the entire work, and (as...

<summary>Agrippa explains that he is publishing this youthful work on magic to prevent "corrupt" and "mangled" versions from being printed by others, while also acknowledging his own later criticisms of the subject.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Agrippa's preface "To the Reader" and begins his formal dedication to his mentor, the Abbot Johannes Trithemius. Agrippa continues to defend the publication of this work, acknowledging that while he once considered "re-weaving the whole web" (completely rewriting it), he has instead chosen to refine and polish his youthful draft. He then transitions into his famous letter to Trithemius, recounting their shared discussions at the monastery in Würzburg and posing the central problem of the book: why the once-venerated art of Magic has fallen into such ill repute.</meta>

& (as they say) to re-weave the whole web, but rather to correct it a little and to infuse it with some splendor. Therefore, kind reader, I ask you once more not to judge these things by the date of this current edition, but to grant indulgence to my curious youth if you happen to find anything here that is less than pleasing.

->**TO THE REVEREND FATHER AND LORD, JOHANNES TRITEMIUS, ABBOT OF SAINT JAMES**<-
->in the suburbs of Würzburg, Henry Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim<-
->sends greetings.<-

**W**HEN I was recently staying with you (reverend father) for some time in your monastery at Würzburg <note>Latin: *Herbipolis*. Trithemius was a famous scholar and cryptographer who mentored the young Agrippa.</note>, and we were conferring together on many things concerning alchemy <note>original: *chimicis*</note>, many things concerning magic, many things concerning the Cabala <note>The "Cabala" (or Kabbalah) refers to a Jewish mystical tradition that Agrippa and other Renaissance humanists adapted into a Christian framework.</note>, and other secret sciences and arts which still lie hidden in mystery: a great question arose among others as to why Magic itself—which once held the highest peak of sublimity in the judgment of all ancient philosophers, and was always held in the highest veneration by those ancient sages and priests—was then always hateful and suspicious to the Holy Fathers from the beginning of the burgeoning Catholic Church, at last rejected by theologians, condemned by sacred canons, and furthermore proscribed by the decrees of all laws. Having pondered the cause of this, in my judgment it is none other than that, by a certain fatal depravity of times and men, many pseudo-philosophers crept in, and under the false name of Magi <note>original: *Magi*. The term refers to the "wise men" or "magicians" of antiquity.</note>, [who following] the sects [of the gentiles] and the detestable superstitions and deadly [rites] <unclear>damaged</unclear> of factions of false religions: [heaping up] wicked sacrileges [against] the orthodox religion, [to the destruction] <unclear>damaged</unclear> of men and injury to God, they published very many books of condemned reading (such as we see circulated today), to which they fixed the most honorable name and title of Magic by theft and robbery. These, therefore...

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory letter from Henry Cornelius Agrippa to his mentor, the Abbot Johannes Trithemius. In the preceding text, Agrippa began discussing the decline of Magic from its ancient status as a revered, sacred science to its current state of ill repute. He now identifies the culprits: those who used the title of "Magic" to mask their own "trifles" and superstitions, leading to the art being condemned as a capital crime.</meta>

...they hoped that they might gain favor for their own cursed trifles under this sacred and holy title of Magic. They have acted in such a way that the name of Magic—once most highly praised—is today rendered most hateful <note>original: *odiosißimum*</note> to all good and honest men. Indeed, it is now considered a capital crime if anyone should dare to profess themselves a mage through their learning or works—unless perhaps it is some senile <note>original: *demēs* (demented or out of her mind)</note> old woman living in the countryside, who wishes to be believed as one quite skilled and divinely powerful. As Apuleius says, such a person claims they can:
->“bring down the sky, suspend the earth, harden fountains, dissolve mountains, raise the spirits of the dead, lower the gods, extinguish the stars, and illuminate Hell itself.”<- <note>original: *poßit cælum deponere, terrā suspēdere, fontes durare, montes diluere, manes sublimare, deos infimare, sydera extinguere, tartarū ipsum illuminare*. This is a famous quote from Apuleius's *Metamorphoses* (The Golden Ass), describing the powers of a witch.</note>
Or as Virgil sings:
    She promises to set free the minds she wishes by her songs,
    But to cast heavy cares upon others,
    To stop the water in rivers, and turn the stars backward;
    She calls forth the spirits of the night; you will see
    The earth groan beneath your feet, and ash trees descend from the mountains. <note>These lines are from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book IV, describing the powers of a Massylian priestess.</note>

Then there are the things Lucan reports concerning that Thessalian witch <note>Referring to the witch Erictho from Lucan's epic poem *Pharsalia*.</note>, and Homer concerning the omnipotence of Circe. I confess that most of these accounts are the products of deceptive opinion, superstitious diligence, and ruinous labors. Because such things cannot fall under a lawful art, they nevertheless presume they can clothe themselves in the venerable title of Magic.

Since matters stood thus, I wondered greatly—and was no less indignant—that until now no one has come forward to vindicate such a sublime and sacred discipline from the charge of impiety, or to hand it down to us in a pure and sincere form. Indeed, among the more recent authors I have seen—Roger Bacon, Robert the Englishman <note>likely Robert of York or Robert of Chester</note>, Peter of Abano, <margin>Authors of Magic</margin> Albert the German <note>Albertus Magnus</note>, Arnald of Villanova, Anselm of Parma, Picatrix the Spaniard <note>The pseudonymous author of the famous grimoire *Picatrix*</note>, Cecco d'Ascoli of Florence, and many others, though writers of obscure name—when they promise to hand down Magic, they provide nothing but certain delusions <note>original: *deliramenta*</note> supported by no reason, or superstitions unworthy of all honest men.

Because of this, my spirit was stirred within me; and because of this mixture of admiration and indignation, I wished to philosophize myself. I did not think I would be performing an unpraiseworthy task, for from my earliest youth I have always been a curious and intrepid explorer of the operations of wonderful effects and those full of mysteries. I sought to determine if I could [rescue] Magic itself—that ancient discipline of all wise men—from [imp... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely heading toward "impiety" or "impurity."</note>]

<summary>Agrippa complains that "Magic" has been dragged through the mud by superstitious frauds and "crazy old women," leading to its legal prohibition. He critiques past authors like Roger Bacon and Albertus Magnus for failing to provide a rational defense of the art, prompting him to write this restoration of "Ancient Magic."</summary>
<keywords>Magic, Superstition, Apuleius, Virgil, Roger Bacon, Albertus Magnus, Peter of Abano, Picatrix, History of Magic, Witchcraft, Natural Philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page concludes Henry Cornelius Agrippa’s dedication to his mentor, the Abbot Johannes Trithemius, and begins Trithemius’s enthusiastic response. Agrippa explains his decision to rename his work to avoid the stigma surrounding "Magic" and asks the Abbot to act as a friendly censor before the work is published.</meta>

...I might restore Magic, purged and crowned of the errors of impiety, adorned with its own proper reasoning, and vindicate it from the injuries of slanderers. Although I have long deliberated upon this within myself, I have never until now dared to descend into this arena; however, after our conversation regarding these matters held at Würzburg <note>original: *Herbipoli*</note>, your own preeminent skill and learning, along with your burning encouragement, added boldness and spirit to my mind. Therefore, having selected the opinions of philosophers of proven faith, and having purged the introductions of malicious men—those who, feigning knowledge, told lies about the traditions of the mages and taught that miraculous operations were to be sought from the very books of darkness that have been condemned, as if from the inner sanctuaries of mysteries—I have, now that the darkness is dispersed, composed in these recent days three books on Magic, gathered into a brief compendium. I have titled them *Of Occult Philosophy*, a less offensive name. I now submit these to your examination, as you hold the fullest expertise in these matters, to be corrected, appraised, and judged. If anything has been written in them by me that might tend toward an insult to nature, an offense to the heavens, or an injury to religion, you may condemn it as an error. If, however, the scandals of impiety are dissolved and purged, you may protect this tradition of truth. Thus, I ask that you deal with these books of ours, and with Magic itself, in such a way that nothing useful is hidden, nor anything approved that can do nothing but harm. In this way, these books, once approved by your examination, may at last be worthy to go forth into the public under happy auspices, fearing no judgment from posterity. Farewell, and be indulgent toward these bold undertakings.

->**JOHANNES TRITEMIUS**<-
->**ABBOT OF SAINT JAMES AT WÜRZBURG,**<-

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page serves as the formal dedicatory epistle of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's "Three Books of Occult Philosophy." It follows the previous page's correspondence where the Abbot Trithemius encouraged Agrippa’s work. Here, Agrippa addresses his patron, Hermann von Wied, the Archbishop of Cologne, offering this monumental work as a scholarly "gift" in exchange for the Prince's protection and favor.</meta>

TO THE MOST REVEREND
FATHER IN CHRIST, AND
MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE
Hermann, Count of Wied, by the grace of God
Archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, Prince-
Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, and Arch-
chancellor throughout Italy, Duke of Westphalia and
Angria, etc. Legate by birth <note>original: *Legato nato*, a title held by certain Archbishops giving them inherent legatine authority</note> of the most Holy
Roman Church, and Vicar General in matters
pontifical, Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
of Nettesheim sends greetings.

**[Initial E]**XCEPTIONAL is the celebrity of your illustrious fame,
most reverend and illustrious Prince,
so great is the magnitude of your virtues and the
splendor of your learning, your frequent practice of
the finest literature, and your grave speech joined with
solid prudence, your elegant readiness
of speech, your knowledge of many things,
your constant religion, and your most praiseworthy character, with which you are endowed above the common custom of others. I say nothing of the ancient images of your eminent nobility, nor the treasures of wealth both old and new, the vastness of your dominion, or the mitres <note>A reference to his high ecclesiastical offices</note> of your sacred dignities—whose excellence you also surpass with the comely form and strength of your body. 

While all these things are indeed very great, I nevertheless judge you to be far greater than all of them because of those heroic and super-illustrious virtues of yours. By these you have surely ensured that the more learned and the more a lover of virtue a person is, the more he desires to find his way into your benevolence. For this reason, I also determined that I must seek that honor of yours for myself, but in the manner of the Parthians—that is, I say, not without a gift. <note>original: *Parthorum more*. Agrippa refers to a historical anecdote where the Parthians never greeted their kings without an offering.</note> Indeed, we see this custom of greeting a Prince derived from the centuries of the ancients down to our own times, and observed even until now. 

And since I saw every other man of remarkable learning adorning you with the beautiful and great gifts of their own scholarship, I did not dare approach your highness with empty hands—as if I alone were a deserter of your honor and veneration. Thus, being thoughtful and looking around within my library for what gift I might be able to present to so distinguished a Prince,

<margin>a 5</margin> behold, among... <note>This "a 5" is a signature mark for the bookbinder, indicating the leaf's position in the printed gathering.</note>

<summary>In this dedicatory preface, Agrippa praises the many virtues, noble lineage, and ecclesiastical power of Hermann von Wied, the Archbishop of Cologne. He frames his scholarly work on occult philosophy as a formal "gift" offered to secure the Prince's patronage, following ancient traditions.</summary>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page concludes the dedicatory epistle from Agrippa to Hermann von Wied. Agrippa explains the provenance of the work, noting that while it began as a youthful project, he has revised and expanded it in his maturity. He seeks the Archbishop's protection against the "envy" (likely religious or academic censorship) that such a controversial topic as magic might provoke.</meta>

...lo, from among my hidden papers, there suddenly appeared the books on **Occult Philosophy**, or on **Magic**, which I had begun to write as a very young man. I had set them aside and forgotten them for many years, but now, out of respect for your Greatness, I have hurried to finish them, as if to fulfill a long-standing vow. I was convinced that I could give you nothing more pleasing than a new work on this most ancient and hidden teaching—a work, I must say, of my inquisitive youth, but a doctrine of antiquity that (I dare say) no one has yet attempted to restore.

Yet, I do not dedicate these writings of mine to you because they are worthy of you, but so that they might open a door for me to your favor. I ask, therefore—if it is not improper—that they might find some excuse in your eyes. I offer you all my prayers, hoping that if these studies of my youth come to light under your Greatness's protection, and if envy is driven away, their memory might endure by the right of eternity. This would bring me the reward of a good conscience, for even now that I am older, many things in these books seem to me both highly useful and necessary to understand.

Thus, you hold a work not only of my youth, but also of my present years. I have corrected many errors of the youthful draft, added insights in many places, and expanded it with many new chapters. You can easily spot these additions by the unevenness of the style <note>original: *orationis inæqualitate*; Agrippa admits that the prose he wrote as a young man differs noticeably from his more mature additions</note>. In this way, you will see that I am devoted to your service throughout my whole life.

Farewell, most happy Prince of happy Cologne.

From Mechelen.
In the year 1531.
In the month of January.

<summary>Agrippa presents his "Three Books of Occult Philosophy" to the Archbishop, explaining that he has revised his youthful drafts into a mature restoration of ancient wisdom. He asks for the Prince's protection for the work and declares his lifelong devotion to the Archbishop's service.</summary>

## BOOK ONE.

### How Mages gather virtues from the triple world will be shown in these three books. CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a figure, possibly a scholar, seated at the foot of a tree within a rural landscape.</image-desc>

Since the world is triple—comprising the elemental, the celestial, and the intellectual—and each lower level is governed by the one above it and receives the influence of its powers, the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The "Archetype" refers to the divine original or the mind of God, which serves as the model for all creation.</note> himself and the supreme Craftsman <note>original: "opifex"</note> pours the virtues of his omnipotence through the angels, the heavens, the stars, the elements, animals, plants, metals, and stones into us, for whose service he founded and created all these things. For this reason, <term>Mages</term> <note>Agrippa uses "Magi" to describe learned practitioners who seek to understand the hidden (occult) workings of the universe.</note> do not think it unreasonable that we can ascend through these same steps, through each individual world, to that very Archetypal world—the Maker of all and the First Cause, from whom all things exist and proceed. They believe we can not only enjoy those powers that already exist in more noble things, but can also draw down new ones from above. Hence, the elemental <note>Catchword: "mundi" (of the world).</note>

### What Magic is, what its parts are, and what kind of person a professor of Magic ought to be. CHAPTER II.

The magical faculty—possessing the greatest power and full of the highest mysteries—embraces the deepest contemplation of the most secret things: the nature, power, quality, substance, and virtue, and the knowledge of all nature. It instructs us how things differ among themselves and how they agree, producing its wonderful effects by uniting the virtues of things through their application to one another, and by coupling and "marrying" <note>original: "maritans." Agrippa uses the metaphor of marriage to describe the joining of lower, earthly substances with higher, celestial influences.</note> lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher things everywhere. This is the most perfect and supreme science, this is the higher and holier philosophy; this, finally, is the absolute consummation of all the most noble philosophy.

...and when dissolved, it becomes water, and when that is thickened and condensed, <margin>it becomes earth</margin> it becomes earth; through heat, however, it evaporates and passes into air, and that air, when overheated, passes into fire; and this fire, when extinguished, returns into air; and when cooled down from excessive burning, it becomes earth, or stone, or sulfur, just as is evident from the effects of lightning. <note>Agrippa is describing the cycle of elemental transformation. The reference to "sulfur" from lightning reflects the historical belief that the "brimstone" smell following a lightning strike was a physical residue of the fire turning into earth.</note> **Plato**, however, believes that earth is entirely transmutable, and that the other elements are transmutable both into it and into each other. Earth is therefore divided by the finer elements—not transformed, but dissolved or mixed into those things which dissolve it, eventually returning to itself. Each of the elements has two specific qualities, the first of which it retains as its own, and in the second it agrees with the following element as a middle ground. For fire is hot and dry, earth is dry and cold, water is cold and moist, and air is <unclear>moist</unclear> and hot. <note>In the Aristotelian system, air is traditionally moist and hot. The OCR text here is damaged but the logic of the "interconnected" qualities requires "moist" to bridge water and fire.</note> In this way, according to two contrary qualities, the elements are contrary to each other: such as fire to water, and earth to air. Furthermore, the elements are opposed in another way: for some are heavy, such as earth and water, and others are light, such as air and fire. For this reason, the **Stoics** <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that held that the universe is composed of active and passive principles.</note> called the former passive and the latter active. Moreover, **Plato**, distinguishing them in another way, assigns three qualities to each: to fire, namely, sharpness, rarity <term>thinness or lack of density</term>, and motion; but to earth, obscurity, density, and rest. According to these qualities, the elements of fire and earth are opposites. The remaining elements borrow qualities from them, so that air receives two qualities of fire—rarity and motion—and one from earth, namely obscurity. Conversely, water receives two from earth—obscurity and density—and one from fire, namely motion. But fire is twice as rare, three times more mobile, and four times sharper than air. Air is twice as sharp, three times rarer, and four times more mobile than water. Consequently, water is twice as sharp as earth, three times rarer, and four times more mobile. In the same way...

### On the threefold reasoning of the elements to be considered. CHAPTER IV.

The four elements we have spoken of are such that without a perfect knowledge of them, we can produce no effect in Magic. However, they are each threefold, so that the <term>quaternary</term> <note>The number four.</note> completes the <term>duodenary</term> <note>The number twelve, often associated with the Zodiac.</note>: and progressing through the <term>septenary</term> <note>The number seven, associated with the planets.</note> into the <term>denary</term> <note>The number ten. Agrippa is referencing Pythagorean numerology where 1+2+3+4=10, the "perfect" number representing the return to unity.</note>, the progression reaches the supreme unity, from which every virtue and marvelous operation depends. In the **first order**, then, the elements are pure; they are neither composed, nor changed, nor do they undergo mixing, but are incorruptible; and they are not the things *from which*, but the things *through which* the virtues of all natural things are produced into effect. Their virtues can be explained by no one: because they can do all things in all things. He who is ignorant of these can reach no operation of marvelous effects. Elements of the **second order** are composite, manifold, various, and impure, yet reducible by art to pure simplicity: when these have returned to their simplicity, their virtue is a completion above all things, giving the finishing touch to all occult operations and operations of nature: and these are the foundation of all natural Magic. Elements of the **third order** are not elements in themselves at first, but are decomposed, varied, manifold, and interchangeable among one another: they are the infallible medium: and therefore they are called the middle

Fire itself is one, and penetrating through all things, as the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed fire was the central element of the universe.</note> say; but in heaven it is expanded and shining; in hell, however, it is contracted, dark, and tormenting; and in the middle, it partakes of both. The properties of the supernal fire are a heat that fertilizes all things and a light that grants life to all. The properties of the infernal fire are a heat that consumes all things and a darkness that fills everything with sterility. Therefore, celestial and bright fire puts to flight dark demons; and our wood-fire also puts them to flight, insofar as it possesses a likeness and a vehicle of that higher light. Moreover, it is a likeness of Him who says: "I am the light of the world," <note>original: "Ego sum lux mundi" (John 8:12).</note> who is the true fire, the "Father of lights," <note>original: "pater luminum" (James 1:17).</note> from whom every best gift comes: emitting and communicating the splendor of His fire.

For this reason, the wisest founders of religions and ceremonies decreed that prayers, psalmody, and all sacred rites should only be performed with lamps lit. Hence that <term>symbol of Pythagoras</term>: <note>Pythagoras was a Greek philosopher whose "symbols" were brief, cryptic maxims for his followers.</note> *Do not speak of God without light.* <note>original: "Ne loquare de deo absque lumine"</note> They also commanded that lights and fires be lit near the bodies of the dead to drive away evil demons, and that they not be removed until the bodies are buried in the earth after the sacred rites of expiation are completed. Even the Almighty in the <term>Old Law</term> <note>The Mosaic Law of the Old Testament.</note> required all His sacrifices to be offered with fire, and that the fire should always burn upon the altar, which the priests of <term>Vesta</term> <note>The Roman goddess of the hearth; her priestesses, the Vestal Virgins, maintained a sacred eternal flame.</note> also kept perpetually among the Romans.

But the basis and foundation of all elements is the Earth. For she is the object, subject, and receptacle of all celestial rays and influences. She contains in herself the seeds and seminal virtues of all things. Therefore, she is called animal, vegetable, and mineral; being fertilized by all the other elements and the heavens, she is the giver of birth to all things from herself. She is the receiver of all fertilities, and like a first parent, she is the bringer-forth of all things, the center, foundation, and mother of all. Take from her whatever is secret, washed, purified, and refined; if you leave it for a time under the open sky <note>original: "sub divo"</note>, it will soon be fertilized and made pregnant by celestial powers, and will of its own self produce plants, worms and animals, stones, and the bright sparks of metals. In her are the greatest secrets, if ever they are [perfected] by art <note>Agrippa refers here to the alchemical "Art," which seeks to refine natural substances to their most potent state.</note>...

## CHAPTER VI. On the Admirable Natures of Water, Air, and the Winds.

The remaining two elements—namely, water and air—are of no less power; nor does nature cease to work miracles within them. For the necessity of water is so great that without it no animal could live; no herb, nor any plant whatsoever, could sprout without the moistening of water. Within it lies the seminal power of all things—firstly in animals, whose seed is clearly watery; but even the seeds of shrubs and herbs, though they may be earthy, must necessarily be softened by water if they are to be fertile, whether that happens through the absorbed moisture of the earth, or by dew, or rain, or water added by design.

The same scripture testifies that even earthly productions are partly owed to water, saying that after creation the shrubs and plants had not germinated because God had not yet rained upon the earth. So great is the power of this element that not even spiritual regeneration <note>The author refers to the Christian sacrament of Baptism.</note> can occur without water, as **Christ** himself testified to **Nicodemus** <note>Referencing the Gospel of John 3:5: "Unless a man be born of water and of the Spirit..."</note>. Its power in religion is also greatest, in expiations and purifications, and its necessity is no less than that of fire. Its utilities are infinite and its use manifold, and all things subsist by its power, as it possesses the strength for generating, nourishing, and increasing. 20          ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY
    How the elements are in the heavens, in the stars, in 
    demons, in angels, and finally in God himself. CAP. VIII.

IT is the unanimous opinion of all the Platonists that, just as in the archetypal world <note>The "archetypal world" refers to the divine blueprint or the mind of God, which contains the perfect forms of all things.</note> all things are in all things, so also in this corporeal world, all things are in all things, though in different ways according to the nature of those things receiving them. Thus, the elements are not only [damaged] in these lower realms, but also in the heavens, in the stars, in demons, in angels, and finally in the very Maker and Archetype of all things. However, in these lower realms, the elements are coarse forms, vast matter, and material elements; but in the heavens, the elements exist through their natures and powers, in a celestial manner and much more excellently than they do beneath the moon. For the solidity of the celestial Earth is there without coarseness; the agility of the Water and Air is far from flowing away; and the heat of the Fire there is not burning, but shining and giving life to all things by its warmth. Furthermore, among the stars, Mars and the Sun are fiery; Jupiter and Venus are airy; Saturn and Mercury are watery; and those which inhabit the eighth sphere <note>The "eighth sphere" or Firmament is the region of the fixed stars, situated beyond the seven planetary spheres.</note> as well as the Moon are earthy (though the Moon is thought by many to be watery). This is because, like the Earth, she attracts the celestial waters; having absorbed them due to her proximity, she flows them into us and communicates them. There are also certain signs among the zodiac that are fiery, some earthy, some airy, and some watery. These govern the elements in the heavens, distributing those four "triplicities" <note>A "triplicity" is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note> into the beginning, middle, and end of each element. Thus, the beginning of Fire is Aries, its progress and increase is Leo, and its end is Sagittarius. The beginning of Earth is Taurus, its progress is Virgo, and its extreme is Capricorn. The beginning of Air is Gemini, its process is Libra, and its boundary is Aquarius. The beginning of Water is Cancer, its middle is Scorpio, and its end is possessed by Pisces. Therefore, from these planets and signs...

<summary>Agrippa explains the Hermetic principle of "as above, so below," arguing that the four elements exist in the heavens and the divine realm in a purified, spiritualized form. He assigns the elements to the planets and the twelve signs of the zodiac according to their triplicities.</summary>

There is also in them an air of subtle spirit, and a love of shining fire; hence they are called in the sacred scriptures "the wings of the wind"; and elsewhere the Psalmist says of them: "Who makes your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire" <note>Psalm 104:4</note>. Of the angelic orders, also, the Seraphim, Virtues, and Powers are fiery; the Cherubim are earthy; the Thrones and Archangels are watery; and the Dominions and Principalities are airy. 

Concerning the Archetype itself, the Maker of all things, is it not read: "Let the earth be opened and bring forth a Savior"? <note>Isaiah 45:8</note> Is it not said of the same: "A fountain of living water, cleansing and regenerating"? <note>Jeremiah 2:13</note> Is not the same the Spirit breathing the "breath of life"; and the same also, as witnessed by Moses and Paul, a "consuming fire"? <note>Deuteronomy 4:24 and Hebrews 12:29</note> Therefore, no one can deny that the elements are found <margin>Elements are present in all things.</margin> everywhere and in all things in their own way: first in these lower things, but drossy and thick,

### Chapter IX.
### On the virtues of natural things which depend most closely on the elements.

<margin>The various natural virtues of things.</margin>

**Natural virtues** of things are partly elemental, such as heating, cooling, moistening, and drying; these are called primary operations or qualities, and also secondary ones. For these qualities alone transform the entire substance, which no other qualities do; they are present in things because of the elements that compose them. Furthermore, there are many other virtues besides the primary qualities, such as those that are maturative <note>ripening or maturing</note>, digestive, <unclear>discutiue</unclear> <note>likely "discutient," meaning to dissipate or scatter morbid matter</note>, mollificative <note>softening</note>, indurative <note>hardening</note>, styptic <note>astringent; contracting tissues to stop bleeding</note>, <unclear>abster</unclear>sive <note>cleansing or wiping away</note>, caustic <note>burning</note>, aperient <note>opening, often referring to the bowels or pores</note>, evaporative, strengthening <note>original: "confortatiue"</note>, conglutinative <note>binding or gluing together</note>, opilative <note>obstructive or clogging</note>, expulsive, attractive <note>original: "attractiue"; drawing inward</note>, repercussive <note>repelling or driving back</note>, stupefactive <note>numbing or dulling the senses</note>, expanding, and many others. For the elemental power in a mixture has much to do which it cannot perform on its own. These are called secondary qualities, because they follow the nature and measure of the mixture of the primary virtues. Much concerning these is found abundantly in the books of physicians. Just as maturation is an operation of natural heat in a certain measure within the substance of matter, so hardening is an operation of cold; likewise freezing and drying. And these operations sometimes act upon specific parts of the body, such as provoking urine, or milk, or the menses; these are called tertiary qualities, which follow the secondary, just as the secondary follow the primary.

There is also a type of flax which Pliny calls asbestos, and the Greeks call *asbeston* <note>original: "ἀσβεστον"; meaning "unquenchable" or "inextinguishable"</note>, which is not consumed by flames; of which Anaxilaus says that a tree wrapped in it can be cut down with silent blows <note>original: "surdis... ictibus"; literally "deaf blows." ### Chapter X.
### On the occult virtues of things.

Moreover, there are in things other virtues which do not belong to any element <note>In this context, "elemental" refers to the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry. Occult virtues are properties that cannot be explained by these four alone</note>, such as putting poison to flight, driving away carbuncles <note>original: "anthraces"; referring to inflammatory sores or boils</note>, attracting iron, or other such effects. This virtue is a consequence of the species and the form of this or that thing. Whence it follows that even in a very small quantity, it has a significant effect in its operation; this is a power not granted to a mere elemental quality.

[A substance] placed above strengthens, placed below draws out: <note>The author is likely referring to the application of specific stones or magnets to the body to either "fix" or "extract" humors.</note> jasper stops bleeding: the echeneis <term>Echeneis: A legendary "suckerfish" (remora) believed by ancient writers like Pliny the Elder to be capable of stopping a massive ship in its tracks by merely clinging to its hull.</term> halts a ship: rhubarb expels bile. 30 OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

The Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: A follower of Aristotle’s philosophy. Agrippa is referring to those who seek purely physical or material explanations for natural phenomena.</term>, relying on his senses and the qualities he can observe, claims these [virtues] arise from the elements and their specific qualities. This might perhaps be thought true, were it not for the fact that physical qualities often belong to the same species, yet the magical operations of stones are many and varied, agreeing neither in species nor in genus. <note>Agrippa argues that if physical heat or cold were the only source of power, then all "hot" things would behave identically; since they don't, there must be a higher, "occult" source.</note> Therefore, the Academics <term>Academics: Followers of Plato’s Academy. In the Renaissance, "Academic" was often synonymous with "Platonist."</term> following Plato attribute these virtues to the "Ideas," the form-givers of things. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian philosopher and physician whose works were central to medieval European science.</note> however, refers them to the Intelligences; Hermes <term>Hermes: Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism, a tradition of Egyptian-Greek wisdom focusing on alchemy, astrology, and theurgy.</term> to the stars; and Albertus [Magnus] to the specific forms of things.

And although these authors seem to oppose one another, none of them, if rightly understood, departs from the truth: since all their sayings agree in many ways toward the same effect. For God, the end and origin of all virtues in the first place, gives the seal of the Ideas to His ministers, the Intelligences. These, like faithful executors, entrust the things committed to them with "ideal" virtue to the heavens and stars as if they were instruments. Meanwhile, they prepare matter to receive those forms which reside in the Divine Majesty—as Plato says in the *Timaeus*—to be drawn down through the stars. The Giver of forms distributes them through the ministry of the Intelligences, whom He has established as rulers and guardians over His works. To these Intelligences, the power over the things committed to them is entrusted, so that every virtue of stones, herbs, metals, and all other things comes from those presiding Intelligences.

Therefore, form and virtue proceed first from the Ideas; then from the presiding and ruling Intelligences; afterward from the aspects of the heavens that dispose them; and further from the disposed temperaments <term>Temperaments: Known in Latin as *complexio*, this refers to the specific mixture and balance of the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) within an object.</term> of the elements that correspond to the influences of the heavens, by which the elements themselves are arranged. Thus, operations of this kind occur in these lower things through the expressed...

<summary>Agrippa argues that the hidden powers of nature cannot be explained by physical elements alone, but result from a hierarchy descending from God and the Ideas through celestial Intelligences and stars down to the material world.</summary>

### BOOK ONE.

*forms, in the heavens through the disposing virtues, in the Intelligences through mediating reasons, and in the Archetype through the Ideas and exemplary forms; all of which must necessarily converge in the effect and execution of the power of every single thing.* <note>Agrippa is describing a "Great Chain of Being." A plant has power because it reflects an Idea in God's mind, passed down through angels (Intelligences) and stars.</note> *Therefore, there is a virtue and a wonderful operation in every herb and stone, but it is greater in a star; beyond which, each thing also acquires much for itself from the presiding Intelligences. But most of all, they come from the Supreme Cause, to whom all things correspond in a mutual and perfect way, ringing out in their own harmonic concord, like certain hymns, always praising that Highest Architect <term>Architect: Original Latin "opificem," referring to God as the master-builder of the universe.</term>, just as in the Chaldean furnace <note>A reference to the biblical story in the Book of Daniel, where three Judean youths were thrown into a furnace by King Nebuchadnezzar but were unharmed and sang a song of praise.</note> they are summoned by those holy youths singing: "Bless the Lord, all things that grow in the earth, and all things that move in the waters, all birds of the heaven, beasts and cattle, together with the sons of men."* <note>original: "Benedicite dominum uniuersa germinantia in terra, & omnia quæ mouentur in aquis, omnes uolucres cæli, bestiæ & pecora simul cum filijs hominum."</note> *Thus, there is no other cause for the necessity of effects than the connection of all things with the First Cause <term>First Cause: A philosophical term for God as the primary source of all movement and existence.</term>, and their correspondence to those divine examples and eternal Ideas; from which every thing has a specific, determined place in the Archetype <term>Archetype: The original model or "blueprint" of the universe existing in the divine mind.</term>, from which it lives and draws its origin. And every virtue of herbs, stones, metals, animals, words, and speeches—and of all things that are from God—is implanted from there. Though He works in these lower things through the Intelligences and the heavens, sometimes God does those things directly by Himself, omitting these intermediaries or suspending their service; these works are then called miracles. For while the secondary causes—which Plato and others call "ministers"—act by necessity and produce their effects necessarily under the command and order of the First Cause, nonetheless, according to His own will, God sometimes so releases or suspends them that they completely cease from the necessity of that command and order.*

<summary>Agrippa explains that all magical power descends from God through a hierarchy of Ideas, Intelligences, and stars, culminating in physical objects. He also distinguishes natural magic (which uses these chains) from miracles (where God bypasses the chain entirely).</summary>

#### Concerning the spirit of the world, what it is, and that it is the vehicle of occult virtues. CHAPTER 14

**Democritus** and **Orpheus**, and the followers of **Pythagoras**, having most diligently scrutinized the powers of celestial and lower things, said that "all things are full of gods." <note>original: "omnia plena dijs esse." They called the divine virtues present in things "gods," which **Zoroaster** <note>A legendary Persian prophet and sage, often cited in the Renaissance as a primary source of ancient wisdom and magic.</note> called "divine allurements," **Synesius** called "symbols," others called "lives," and still others called "souls." They said that the virtues of things depend upon this: that from one single matter, powers are extended into other things; just as a human extends the intellect toward things that can be understood, and the imagination toward things that can be imagined. ### How we ought to investigate and experiment with the virtues of things, through the way taken from similarity. CHAPTER XV.

It is therefore clear that the **hidden properties** in things are not implanted by elemental nature, but from heaven; they are hidden from our senses and barely known even to reason. These indeed proceed from the life and spirit of the world through the very rays of the stars, and they can be investigated by us in no other way than through experience and conjecture. Whence, O seeker <note>original: "cupiens." Literally "the one desiring," a common way of addressing a student of the hermetic arts.</note>, you who desire to work in this study, you ought to consider that every single thing moves and converts toward its likeness, and inclines toward itself according to its whole power, both in property (that is, in **hidden virtue**) as well as in quality (that is, in **elemental virtue**). 

Sometimes [this occurs] even in the substance itself, as we see in salt: for whatever stands with salt for a long time becomes salt. For every agent, when it begins to act, does not move toward something inferior to itself, but in some way, as far as possible, toward its equal and correspondent. We see this clearly in sentient animals, in whom the nutritive virtue does not transmute food into grass or a plant, but converts it into sentient flesh. ### How the virtues of things are to be investigated and tested through strife and friendship. CHAPTER XV.

It remains now to see how all things possess within themselves friendship and enmity. Every thing has <note>original: "habet"; text is damaged in original</note> something to be feared and dreaded—an enemy and a destructive <note>original: "destructiuum"; text is damaged</note> force; and on the contrary, something exulting, gladdening, and comforting. In the elements, fire is opposed to water, and air to earth; the others agree with one another. Again, among the heavenly bodies, the friends of Saturn are Mercury, Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon; his enemies are Mars <note>original: "Martem"; text is damaged</note> and Venus. All planets are friends of Jupiter except Mars <note>original: "Martem"; text is damaged</note>. Likewise, all things hold Mars in hatred except Venus. The Sun is loved by Jupiter and Venus, while Mars, Mercury, and the Moon are hostile to it. All love Venus except Saturn. The friends of Mercury are Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn; his enemies are the Sun, Moon, and Mars. However, the friends of the Moon are Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn; her enemies are Mars and Mercury. 

There is another enmity between stars, namely when they possess opposite <term>houses</term> <note>In astrology, a "house" or domicile is the zodiac sign over which a planet has natural lordship. Enmity occurs when planets rule signs directly across from each other on the zodiac wheel.</note>, such as Saturn against the <term>luminaries</term> <note>The Sun and Moon.</note>, Jupiter against Mercury, and Mars against Venus. An even stronger enmity exists between those whose <term>exaltations</term> <note>An "exaltation" is a specific sign where a planet’s influence is thought to be most harmoniously or powerfully expressed.</note> are opposite: such as Saturn and the Sun, Jupiter and Mars, or Venus and Mercury. 

But the strongest friendship is among those who agree in nature, quality, substance, and power—such as Mars with the Sun, Venus with the Moon, and likewise Jupiter with Venus. There is also a friendship between those whose exaltation is in the house of another: such as Saturn with Venus, Jupiter with the Moon, Mars with Saturn, the Sun with Mars, Venus with Jupiter, and the Moon with Venus. And of what kind the friendships and enmities of the higher things are, such are the inclinations of the things subject to them in these lower realms. ...than certain inclinations of things toward each other, desiring such or such <unclear>condition</unclear> if it be absent, moving toward it unless hindered, resting once it is attained, fleeing its contrary, dreading its proximity, and finding no rest within it. Led by this opinion, Heraclitus declared that all things come to be through strife and friendship. 

Indeed, these inclinations of friendship are found in plants and minerals, such as the attraction the magnet has for iron; the emerald for riches and favor; jasper for childbirth; and agate for eloquence. In a similar way, naphtha <note>A flammable petroleum distillate known in antiquity for its "attraction" to fire.</note> draws fire to itself, leaping toward it from wherever it is seen; likewise, the root of the *aproxis* <note>A legendary herb described by Pliny the Elder that ignites from a distance when near fire.</note> herb draws fire from afar just as naphtha does. 

A similar inclination exists between the male and female palm tree; when the branch of one touches the branch of the other, they fold themselves into a mutual embrace. The female palm bears no fruit without the male, and even a solitary almond tree is less fruitful. Vines love the elm and the maple <note>original: "opium"; likely referring to the Field Maple (*Acer campestre*), which was traditionally used as a living support for grapevines.</note>, and the olive tree and the myrtle share a mutual affection; the same is true for the olive and the fig. 

Among animals, friendship exists between the blackbird and the thrush, the crow and the heron, and between peacocks and doves, or turtledoves and parrots. Whence Sappho <note>Though attributed here to Sappho, these lines are from Ovid’s *Heroides* 15, written in the voice of Sappho to her lover Phaon.</note> writes to Phaon:

*To various birds are white doves often joined,* <note>original: "Et uarijs albæ iunguntur ſæpe columbæ"</note>
*And the black turtledove is loved by the green bird.* <note>original: "Et niger à uiridi turtur amatur aue."</note>

Again, the pilot-fish <note>original: "musculus"; a small fish believed by ancients to guide whales and protect them from running aground.</note> and the whale are friends. <margin>The friendship of animals with other things.</margin> Nor is there only friendship among animals themselves, but also with other things, such as with metals, stones, and plants. For example, the cat rejoices in the herb catnip <note>original: "nepta"; catmint or catnip.</note>, by the rubbing of which it is said to conceive and thus supply the absence of a male. Likewise, mares in Cappadocia expose themselves to the blast of the wind, and through its breath and attraction, they are said to conceive. So too, frogs, toads, snakes, and all kinds of venomous reptiles rejoice in the plant called "laughter's parsley" <note>original: "apium risus"; likely the *Ranunculus sceleratus* or Cursed Buttercup, which was thought to cause a fatal, involuntary contraction of the facial muscles resembling a grin—the "sardonic laugh."</note>...

### On the inclinations of enmities. CHAPTER XVIII.

Conversely, there are the inclinations of enmities. These are natural inclinations similar to hatred, such as anger, indignation, and a certain commanding contrariety, by which a thing flees its opposite and repels it, as if things were fleeing from its very face. Such inclinations are possessed by rhubarb against yellow bile; <note>original: "choleram"; in the humoral system, yellow bile was associated with fire and heat.</note> theriac <note>original: "theriaca"; a famous poly-pharmaceutical "universal" antidote.</note> against poison; sapphire against carbuncles, <note>original: "anthracem"; referring here to inflammatory skin ulcers or "carbuncles" rather than the modern disease anthrax.</note> febrile heats, and ailments of the eyes; amethyst against drunkenness; jasper against the flow of blood and harmful phantasms; emerald and *agnus castus* <note>original: "agnus castus"; the chaste tree, believed since antiquity to suppress sexual desire.</note> against lust; agates against poisons; Peony against the falling sickness; <note>original: "morbum caducum"; an old term for epilepsy.</note> coral against the illusions of black bile <note>original: "atrae bilis"; melancholy.</note> and pains of the stomach; topaz against spiritual heats, such as avarice, luxury, and all excesses of love. 

A similar inclination exists in ants toward the herb marjoram, the wing of a bat, and the heart of a hoopoe, from whose presence they flee. Marjoram is also contrary to "sun-fleers" <note>original: "solifugis"; a term used for spiders or venomous insects that avoid the light.</note> and it resists salamanders. It disagrees with cabbage with such a persistent hatred that they destroy one another. Likewise, cucumbers so hate oil that they curve themselves into a hook so as not to touch it. It is also said that the gall of a crow puts people to flight and frightens them away from a place where it has been hidden with certain other things. 

In the same way, the diamond <note>original: "adamas"</note> is at odds with the magnet, so that when placed nearby, it does not allow iron to be attracted. And sheep flee from frog-parsley <note>original: "apium raninum"; likely *Ranunculus sceleratus*, the celery-leaved buttercup, which is toxic to livestock.</note> as if it were deadly; and what is even more wonderful, nature has painted a sign of this death upon the livers of the sheep, in which the figure of the frog-parsley is found naturally described...

44 ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

### How the virtues of things are to be investigated and tested, which belong to them from their whole species, or are born into a certain thing by the particular gift of the individual itself. CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>Virtues belong to things in two ways.</margin>Furthermore, you ought to consider that the virtues of things belong to certain [creatures] according to their species: such as boldness and high spirits in the lion and the rooster, timidity in the hare and the lamb, rapacity or greed in the wolf, craftiness and deceit in the fox, fawning in the dog, avarice in the raven and the crow, pride in the horse, anger in the tiger and the wild boar, sadness and melancholy in the cat, and lust in the sparrow, and so on with similar cases. For the greatest part of natural virtues accompanies the species. Some, however, belong to things according to the individual, just as there are certain people who vehemently abhor the sight of a cat, so much so that they cannot look at it without the most serious horror—which horror indeed does not belong to them according to the human species, as is manifest. And Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician and philosopher.</note> relates that in his own time a man lived whom all venomous things fled, while everything died that happened to bite him, though he himself remained entirely unharmed. And Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the German Dominican friar and polymath known for his work in the natural sciences.</note> reports that in Cologne <note>original: "Agrippina Colonia"</note> he saw a girl who hunted spiders for food, and being remarkably delighted by that kind of nourishment, was well nourished. Thus there is boldness in the prostitute and timidity in the thief. And in this way philosophers say that an individual who has never suffered illness provides a cure for every illness; therefore they say that the bone of a dead man who never had fevers, when hung over a patient, frees them from a quartan fever <note>A fever recurring every third day, historically associated with malaria.</note>. There are also many singular virtues in individuals, infused by the celestial bodies, as we have shown above.

### That natural virtues reside in some things through their entire substance, but in others within certain specific parts or members. CHAPTER XX.

Again you ought to consider that the virtues of things reside in some according to the whole—that is, according to their whole substance or all its parts. For instance, that little fish, the echeneis <term>echeneis: also known as the remora or "ship-holder," a fish believed in antiquity to be capable of stopping a ship's progress by simply clinging to its hull</term>, which is said to stop a ship by touch alone; it does not perform this action through any one specific part, but through its entire substance. Thus the hyena possesses this property throughout its whole substance: that by the mere contact of its shadow, dogs are struck dumb. So too celandine <term>chelidonia: the Greater Celandine herb, long used in folk medicine</term> benefits the eyesight, not through any single part, but through all its parts—no less in the root than in the leaves and the seed—and so it is with similar things.

Some virtues, however, reside in things according to certain of their parts: for example, only in the tongue, or the eyes, or other specific members or portions. Thus, in the eyes of the basilisk <term>basilisk: a mythical serpent-king said to kill with its gaze</term> and the catablepas <term>catablepas: a legendary Ethiopian beast described by Pliny as having a heavy head and a gaze that turns onlookers to stone or kills them</term> there is a most violent power of killing men as soon as it sees them. A similar power is found in the eyes of the hyena; whatever animal it gazes upon immediately freezes, is dazed, and cannot move itself. A similar power is in the eyes of certain wolves, who, if they see someone first, the person becomes stunned and grows so hoarse that if they wish to shout, they lose the use of their voice. Virgil mentions this when he sings:

*The voice itself has now fled Moeris; the wolves saw Moeris first.* <note>original: "Vox quoque Moerim / Iam fugit ipsa, lupi Moerim videre priores." From Virgil's Eclogues 9.53–54, referencing the Roman folk belief that a wolf's gaze could steal a man's speech.</note>

So too there were certain women in Scythia, and among the Illyrians and Triballi, who are said to have killed whenever they looked upon someone in anger. <margin>Why fascinators use the eyes especially, and not other parts.</margin> Similarly, it is read that the Telchines <note>The Telchines were mythical inhabitants of Rhodes, known as skilled metalworkers and sorcerers who were eventually destroyed by the gods for their malevolence.</note> were a people of Rhodes who changed all things for the worse with their gaze, for which reason they were drowned by Jupiter. Therefore, fascinators <term>fascinatores: those who practice "fascination," a form of magic or the "evil eye" that works through the power of sight</term> of this kind...

### Of the virtues of things which are in them during life, and those which remain in them even after death. CHAPTER XXI.

From this it follows that just as the eagle in its life surpasses and conquers all other birds, so even after it is dead, its feathers destroy and corrode the quills and feathers of other birds. In a similar way, a drum made from the skin of a <unclear>sea-urchin</unclear> <note>original: "ericij marini," literally a "sea-hedgehog"</note> puts all reptiles to flight from a distance, as far as such a sound can be heard. And it is manifest that strings made from the intestines of a wolf, if they are stretched on a lyre or lute alongside strings of sheep-gut, can produce no harmony.

### How inferior things [are subject to] the celestials, and how the activities and m[embers] of men are distributed.

It is manifest that all [inferior things are subject to] those above, and in a certain way [all things] are present in each other; namely, the highest things in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest. Thus in heaven there are earthly things, but in a celestial manner and cause; and on earth there are celestial things, but in a terrestrial manner, namely, according to their effect. Thus we say there are certain solar beings here, and certain lunar ones, in which the Sun and Moon cause something of their own virtue. Hence things of this sort receive many operations and properties similar to the operations of the stars and constellations <note>original: "figurarum"</note> under which they fall.

So we know solar things relate to the heart and the head, because of Leo (the house of the Sun) and Aries (the Sun's exaltation). Likewise, things of Mars <note>original: "martialia"</note> contribute to the head and the testicles, because of Aries and Scorpio. From this, for those who are intoxicated with wine, whose senses stagger and whose head aches, placing the testicles in cold water or washing them with vinegar is an immediate remedy. <note>This medical advice is based on the astrological link between the signs Aries (the head) and Scorpio (the genitals), both of which are ruled by the planet Mars. Treating one "Martial" part was thought to affect the other.</note>

But regarding these matters, it is necessary to know how the human body is distributed among the planets and signs. Know therefore, according to the tradition of the Arabs, that the Sun presides over the brain, the heart, the thigh, the marrow, the right eye, and the spirit of life. To the tongue, however, and the mouth, and the other instruments or organs of the senses, both internal and external—furthermore to the hands, feet, legs, nerves, and the <term>Phantastic virtue: the power of the imagination (phantasia) to form and store mental images.</term>—Mercury presides.

Saturn <margin>Why the image of the navel was in the temple of Jupiter Ammon.</margin> presides over the spleen, the <unclear>milt</unclear> <note>original: "lieni"</note>, the stomach, the bladder, the womb, and the right ear, and over the receptive power itself. Jupiter presides over the liver and the fleshier part of the stomach, as well as the belly and the navel; hence in the temple of Jupiter Ammon, an image of a navel [was worshiped].

## How it is to be known which natural things are subject to which stars, and what things belong to each. CHAPTER XXII

Identifying which thing is subject to which star or zodiac sign is indeed very difficult; however, they are recognized by means of the rays, the movement, or the shapes of the higher celestial bodies. They are also known through colors and odors, and some even through the effects of their operations which harmonize with certain stars. 

Solar things <note>Things belonging to the Sun; original: "Solaria"</note> among the elements are fire and the bright flame; in bodies, the purer blood and the spirit of life; among flavors, the sharp mixed with sweetness. Among metals, gold is Solar because of its brilliance and splendor; and it possesses from the Sun the quality of being a strengthener of the heart. Among stones, those are Solar which imitate the sun’s rays with golden droplets: such as the stone *aëtites* <note>The "eagle-stone," traditionally believed to be found in eagles' nests; original: "aëtites"</note>, which, by imitating the Sun with its golden specks, has power against the falling sickness <note>Epilepsy; original: "morbum caducum"</note> and against poison. So too is the stone called the *Eye of the Sun* <note>original: "Solis oculus"</note>, which has a shape similar to an eye, from the middle of which a ray flashes forth; it strengthens the spirit and aids the sight. Likewise, the carbuncle <note>A red gemstone, often garnet or ruby, once believed to glow in the dark</note>, shining at night, has power against all poisonous and vaporous air. 

<margin>The Chrysolite stone.</margin> So also the *chrysolite* stone, having a thin and shining color, in which a golden star flashes when it is held up to the Sun; it strengthens the spiritual parts <note>The vital organs or "spirits" of the body</note> and assists those with asthma. When it is bored through and the hole is filled with the bristles of a donkey and tied to the left arm, it puts to flight phantasms and melancholic terrors, and repels sadness. 

<margin>The Iris stone.</margin> So too the *Iris* stone, similar in color to crystal; it is frequently found in a hexagonal shape, and when it is held up to the rays of the Sun, with one part kept in the shade, it gathers the solar rays into itself, which it reflects and projects, making a rainbow <note>original: "Irim"</note> appear on the opposite wall. Likewise the *heliotrope* <note>Often called "bloodstone" today; original: "heliotropius"</note>, a green stone in the manner of jasper or emerald, marked with red drops...

### What things are under Saturn. CAP. XXV.

**Saturnine** things among the elements are earth and also water: among the humors, moist black bile <note>melancholy</note>, both natural and adventitious <note>acquired through diet or illness</note>, except for the scorched variety. ->**That the whole sublunary world, and everything in it, is distributed among the planets. CHAPTER 30.**<-

Furthermore, whatever is found in the entire world is formed according to the rule of the planets and receives power from them. Thus, in fire, the life-giving light is attributed to the Sun, while heat is attributed to Mars. On Earth, the varied surface belongs to the Moon, Mercury, and the starry heaven, while the entire mass belongs to Saturn. But in the middle elements <note>Air and water, which sit between the "heaviness" of earth and the "lightness" of fire.</note> where they rule, the airy moisture is subject to Jupiter, while the watery moisture is subject to the Moon, and the mixed moisture obeys Mercury and Venus. By a similar reasoning, moving causes <note>The active forces that make things happen.</note> in nature follow the Sun, while matter follows the Moon; the fertility of moving causes follows Jupiter, and the fertility of matter follows Venus. A swift progress toward an effect follows Mars and Mercury—the former because of his intensity, the latter because of his dexterity and many-sided power. However, the permanent continuation of all things is dedicated to Saturn. Moreover, among the number of plants, everything that bears fruit belongs to Jupiter, and everything that bears flowers belongs to Venus; all seeds and bark belong to Mercury, while every root belongs to Saturn, all wood to Mars, and the leaves to the Moon. Hence, all things that bear fruit but do not flower belong to Saturn and Jupiter; while those that flower...

### On the seals and characters of natural things. CHAPTER XXXIII.

**All stars** have their own proper natures, properties, and conditions: whose **seals** <note>original: "signacula"</note> and **characters** they produce through their rays even in these lower things—in the elements, in stones, in plants, in animals, and in their various members. Whence each and every thing, by a harmonic disposition and from its own star irradiating it, obtains some **special seal** or **character** impressed upon itself. <margin>Every thing has its own character.</margin> This mark is significant of that star or harmony, and contains within itself a **special virtue** <note>a hidden power or efficacy</note> that differs from others, whether by its genus, its species, or the specific arrangement of its underlying matter. Therefore, every thing has its own character for some peculiar effect impressed upon it by its own star, especially by that which holds primacy over it above the rest. These characters contain and retain within themselves the proper natures, virtues, and roots of their stars, and they produce similar operations in other things upon which they are reflected, and of their stars...

->On the mixing of natural things together, and their utility. CHAPTER XXXV.<-

We have discovered that in lower nature, all the gifts of the higher bodies <note>The "higher bodies" are the planets and stars.</note> are not found contained within one single thing, but are dispersed among many species here with us. For example, there are many solar things, yet each of them does not embrace all the virtues <note>original: "uirtutes"; the inherent powers or properties of a thing.</note> of the Sun; rather, one has some properties from the Sun, and another has others. Therefore, it is sometimes necessary to make mixtures in our operations, so that if a hundred or a thousand solar virtues are scattered through as many plants, animals, and similar things, we can fuse them together and reduce them into one form, in which we will see all those said virtues now contained as one. 

<margin>Twofold power in a mixture.</margin> Furthermore, there is a twofold power in a mixture: one, namely, which was previously implanted in its parts and is celestial, the other [arising] through a certain and skillful [mixing] of many things together.
