<margin>How such things [are given] from natural things</margin>

**D**ietary laws and the teachings of the Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmanas"; referring to the ancient Indian philosophers and priests often cited in Renaissance occultism for their perceived ancient wisdom.</note> confess that all things which are in this world of generation <note>the physical world where things are born and die</note> also exist in the celestial world, though with a clearer mark, and in the intellectual world in a most perfect <unclear>order</unclear>. They explain that each inferior thing in the series corresponds to its superior, and through that to the supreme, according to its kind. From these superiors, things below receive that celestial power from the heavens—which they call the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quintam essentiam"; also known as the ether, the pure substance of the stars that permeates all things</note>, or the spirit of the world, or the middle nature. From the intellectual world, they receive a spiritual and living vigor that transcends every quality of virtue. Finally, from the archetype <note>the divine original pattern in the mind of God</note>, they receive through these intermediaries the original power of all perfection, according to their degree. Hence, every single thing can be aptly traced back from these inferior realms to the stars, from the stars to their respective Intelligences <note>the angelic beings believed to guide the celestial bodies</note>, and from there to the archetype itself. From this series, all magic and every more occult philosophy flows.

<margin>Whence magic flows.</margin>

For daily, something natural is drawn out through art, and daily something divine is drawn through nature. The Egyptians, observing this, called nature a "magician" <note>original: "maga"</note>; that is, they recognized the magic power itself in the attraction of like by like, and of harmonious things by harmonious things. This kind of attraction, occurring through the mutual harmony of things toward one another—of the higher with the lower—the Greeks called <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: Greek "συμπαθείαν" (sympatheian); the concept that all parts of the universe are interconnected and affect one another</note>. matter: for fire is not mixed with water, except through the mediation of air, nor is air mixed with earth, except through water. In the same way, the soul is not joined to the body except through the <term>spirit</term> <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to a subtle, thin vapor or "pneuma" that Renaissance philosophers believed acted as a bridge between the physical body and the non-physical soul.</note>; nor is the intellect joined to the spirit except through the soul. By these examples, we see how, through certain natural and artificial preparations, we are able to receive certain celestial gifts from above. For stones and metals correspond with herbs, and herbs with animals, and animals indeed with the heavens; these in turn correspond with the <term>Intelligences</term> <note>original: "intelligentijs"; the angelic beings or celestial minds believed to govern the movements of the planets and stars.</note>, and these with the divine properties and attributes, and finally with God himself, in whose likeness and image all things were created. 

The first image of God is the world; the image of the world is man; of man, the animal; of the animal, the <term>zoophyte</term> <note>original: "zoophytum"; a term for organisms perceived to be on the boundary between animals and plants, such as coral or sea sponges.</note>; of the zoophyte, the plant; of the plant, metals; and of these, stones represent their similarities and reflections.

Divinity is linked to the mind, the mind to the intellect, the intellect to the intention, the intention to the imagination, the imagination to the faculty of sensation, sensation to the senses, and these finally to physical things.

**The Magi** <note>original: "Magi"; here referring to practitioners of "natural magic" who study the hidden properties of the universe.</note> teach that through lower things that conform to higher things, celestial gifts can be drawn down by the opportune influences of heaven. In this way, through these celestial influences, celestial <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "daemones"; in Renaissance philosophy, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or spiritual intelligences that govern the stars and planets.</note>—acting as the attendants of the stars—can be reconciled and introduced to us.

Therefore, when certain materials possessing a natural divine power (that is, things which are naturally in harmony with the higher powers) are properly collected and opportunely blended together from all sides, not only vital, but even intellectual and divine gifts can be received from above. **Synesius** <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a Neo-Platonic philosopher and bishop.</note>, along with the entire school of Platonists, confirms this; and **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>The legendary sage and supposed author of the Hermetic corpus, central to Western occultism.</note> writes that from specific and certain things that correspond to a particular spirit, a statue that is properly composed is immediately animated by that corresponding spirit. **Augustine** also mentions this in the eighth book of *The City of God* <note>St. Augustine discusses (and critiques) the Egyptian practice of "drawing down" spirits into statues as described in the Hermetic texts.</note>. 

For such is the harmony of the world that even super-celestial things are drawn by celestial ones, and supernatural things harmonize with and are drawn by natural ones. This is because a single <term>creative power</term> <note>original: "virtus opifex"; the active, formative force of the Creator that shapes the world according to divine patterns.</note> and a participation in the [Platonic] forms is diffused through all things. This creative power, just as it produces manifest things from hidden causes, so it attracts hidden things through manifest ones <margin>The Magus attracts hidden things through manifest ones.</margin>: for instance, through the rays of the stars, through <term>suffumigations</term> <note>The ritual burning of specific herbs or incense to attract planetary influences.</note>, through lights, through sounds, and through natural things.

<margin>Animals can be recalled to life; man, not so easily.</margin>

Thus, flies that have been drowned, if they are placed in warm ashes, revive; and drowned bees likewise recover their life in the juice of **catmint** <note>original: "nepeta".</note>; and eels dead from a lack of water, if their body remains intact and they are placed under dung in vinegar, and some vulture's blood is added, after a few days they all recover their life. We know also that the **pelican** recalls its killed chicks to life with its own blood. <note>The pelican "in her piety" was a common medieval and Renaissance symbol for Christ, based on the belief that it would peck its own breast to revive its young with blood.</note>

### On bindings, of what sort they are, and by what means they are accustomed to be made. CHAPTER <note>This is Chapter 40 of Book I.</note>

It has been said concerning the virtues and wonderful efficacy of natural things. It now remains to see a matter of great wonder, and that is the binding <term>ligatio; the magical act of "tying" or constraining a person, object, or force through occult means</term> <margin>Multiple types of binding.</margin> of humans into love or into hatred, into sickness and health, and such like. Likewise the binding of thieves and robbers, so that in a certain place they cannot steal; the binding of merchants, so that in a certain place they cannot buy or sell; the binding of an army, so that it cannot cross some boundary; the binding of ships, so that by no force of the winds—even with infinite sails stretched by the wind—are they at all able to leave the harbor. Likewise the binding of a mill, so that it can be turned by no force; the binding of a cistern or fountain, so that water cannot be drawn from it; the binding of a field, so that crops cannot be produced in it; the binding of a certain place, so that nothing can be built in it; the binding of fire, so that in a certain place it cannot be lit, and so that some combustible material, even with the strongest fire applied, does not burn.

Likewise the binding of lightning and storms, so they cannot harm. Likewise the binding of dogs, so they cannot bark; the binding of birds and wild beasts, so they cannot fly or flee; and things similar to these which are scarcely believable, but which nevertheless have very often been known through experience. 

<margin>Through what things bindings are made.</margin> Now, bindings of this kind are made through sorceries <term>veneficia; specifically refers to magic involving drugs, poisons, or potions</term>, through eye-salves <note>original: "collyria"</note>, ointments, potions or philtres, through tying and hanging <note>Referring to "alligationes & suspensiōes," the practice of wearing charms or amulets around the neck or bound to the body.</note>, through rings, through fascinations <note>original: "fascinationes"; the power of the "evil eye" or the gaze to influence others</note>, through strong imaginations and ecstasies of the mind <note>original: "animi excessus"</note>, through images and characters, through incantations and imprecations, through lights, through sounds, through numbers, through words and names, invocations, sacrifices...

<summary>This page introduces the concept of "binding" (ligatio), a form of magic used to constrain or inhibit people, animals, and natural forces. Agrippa lists numerous applications—from stopping ships and fires to influencing human emotions—and identifies the various tools used to achieve these effects, such as potions, rings, and incantations.</summary>

**Certain suffumigations** <note>The ritual burning of incense, herbs, or other substances to produce smoke.</note> adapted to the stars are also very powerful, insofar as they vehemently affect the air and the spirit <note>original: *spiritum*</note> so that they might opportunely seize celestial gifts under the rays of the stars: for our own spirit is greatly transformed by vapors of this kind, since both are a type of vapor and similar to one another. <margin>Suffumigation conducive to prophecy.</margin>

Truly, let no one wonder how much suffumigations can do in the air, who perceives with **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote extensively on theurgy and the nature of spirits.</note> that by certain vapors exhaling from their proper suffumigations, **airy spirits** <note>original: *daemones*</note> are immediately enticed and insinuated, and thunders and lightnings are induced, and similar things: just as it is well known that the **liver of a chameleon** burnt upon the highest roof-tiles incites rains and lightnings: similarly the **head and throat**, if they are set on fire with **oak wood**, cause the shocks of rains and thunders.

**Suffumigations** <note>The practice of burning substances to create smoke for ritual or medicinal purposes.</note> are also performed under the favorable influences of the stars, causing images of spirits to appear in the air or elsewhere. Thus they say that if a fume is made from **coriander**, **henbane** <note>original: *hyoscyamo*; a highly toxic plant in the nightshade family used historically for its hallucinogenic properties</note>, and **hemlock** <note>original: *cicuta*</note>, spirits will immediately gather; 

<margin>Gathering of spirits; hence they call those the herbs of spirits.</margin>

for this reason, they call these the **herbs of spirits**. Conversely, they say that if a fume is made from the **root of the giant fennel** <note>original: *cannæ ferulæ*</note> with the juice of **hemlock**, **henbane**, **mullein** <note>original: *tassi, barbassi*; likely a corruption of *tapsus barbatus*</note>, and **red and black sandalwood**, it makes strange shapes and figures appear. And if **celery** <note>original: *apii*; can also mean parsley</note> is added to these, it drives away spirits from every place and destroys their illusions. Furthermore, a fume made from **calaminth**, **peony**, **mint**, and **palm** <note>original: *pasti*; likely referring to dates or a preparation of palm</note> puts to flight all evil spirits and harmful phantoms.

Additionally, it is recorded that certain animals are summoned or driven away by specific fumes. For instance, it is said that by burning the **liparis** <note>A legendary stone or perhaps a type of fish mentioned by ancient writers like Pliny</note>, all beasts are called forth. Likewise, it is said that **snakes** are gathered by the fumes of a **deer’s throat**, but are put to flight by the burning of **deer horn**. The burning of **peacock feathers** produces the same effect. Similarly, they say that all poisonous things flee from the burning **lung of a donkey**; and if the **hoof of a horse** is burned in a house, the **mice** are driven away. The same is said to happen with the **hoof of a mule**. Even **flies** are driven away if the **left foot** <note>The text is incomplete here, likely referring to the foot of a wolf or a similar creature based on contemporary grimoires.</note> is burned. 

Furthermore, if a house or any place is fumigated with the **ink of a cuttlefish** <note>original: *atramento sepiæ*</note> mixed with **incense** <note>original: *thymi amate*; likely *thymiama*</note>, **roses**, and **aloes**, and if some **rainwater** or **blood** is then sprinkled in that place, the whole house will appear to be full of blood; and if **plowed earth** is thrown there, the earth will seem to tremble. Vapors of this kind infuse a certain body and power into the air and remain there for a very long time. This should be considered no different than how a **contagious or poisonous vapor** of a plague, even if kept in a house for more than two years <unclear>unseen</unclear>, infects the inhabitants, just as happens in an epidemic.

And it must be known that just as there is opposition and enmity among the stars and spirits, so it is also with the fumes used for them. For instance, **aloe wood** and **sulfur** oppose each other, as do **frankincense** and **mercury** <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note>. Spirits brought in by a fume of aloe wood will flee as soon as sulfur is lit. This is like the example Proclus <note>A late Neoplatonic philosopher (412–485 AD) known for his work on the "theurgy" or divine magic.</note> gives of a spirit that used to appear in the form of a **lion**, but vanished as soon as a **rooster** was presented, because the rooster is the lion's opposite. Such principles must be considered and put into practice.

The composition of certain highly 
appropriate suffumigations. CHAPTER XLIV <note>The Roman numeral is damaged in the original, but this is Chapter 44 of the first book.</note>

Thus we prepare a suffumigation for the **Sun** using **ambergris**, **musk**, **aloe wood**, **balsam wood**, and **laurel bark**, with **cloves**, **myrrh**, and **frankincense**. These are crushed and mixed in a certain proportion so that their power yields a sweeter scent; they are then incorporated with **eagle's brain** <note>original: *aquilae*</note> or the **blood of a white rooster**, in the manner of pills or troches <note>Small medicated lozenges or cakes intended to be burned or dissolved.</note>.

However, we prepare the **Lunar** <note>Associated with the Moon.</note> suffumigation from the **dried head of a frog**, **bull's eyes**, and **poppy seed**, with **frankincense** and **camphor**, which shall be incorporated with **menstrual blood** or the **blood of a goose**.

For **Saturn**, one takes the seed of the **black poppy**, **henbane** <note>original: *hyoscyami*; a toxic plant in the nightshade family used for its sedative and hallucinogenic properties.</note>, **mandrake root**, **loadstone** <note>A naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite.</note>, and **myrrh**; these are prepared with the **brain of a cat** or the **blood of a bat**.

For **Jupiter**, one takes **ash tree seed**, **aloe wood**, **benzoin gum**, **lapis lazuli**, and the **crests of a peacock**; these are incorporated with the **blood of a stork** or a **swallow**, or with **deer brain**.

For **Mars**, we take **euphorbium**, **bdellium** <note>A semi-transparent oleo-gum resin similar to myrrh.</note>, **gum ammoniac**, the **roots of both hellebores** <note>Both the Black Hellebore and White Hellebore, plants traditionally used in medicine and magic for purging and protection.</note>, **loadstone**, and a quantity of **sulfur**; all these are incorporated with the **brain of a wolf**, **human blood**, and the **blood of a black cat**.

For **Venus**, we prepare a fumigant from **musk**, **aloe wood**, **red roses**, and **red coral**; these are prepared with the **brains of sparrows** and the **blood of doves**.

For **Mercury**, a suffumigation is made from **mastic**, **frankincense**, **cloves**, and the herb **cinquefoil** <note>original: *pentaphyllo*; literally "five leaves," a common plant in folk magic.</note>, as well as **agate stone**. All these are incorporated with the **brain of a fox** or a **weasel**, and with the **blood of a magpie**.

->## Concerning physical bindings and suspensions. CHAPTER XL<-

When the Soul of the World <note>original: *Anima mundi*; the vital spirit or force that many Renaissance philosophers believed animated all matter in the universe.</note>, through its power, gives [properties] to things naturally generated or artificially made, infusing into them celestial qualities for the wonderful effects they perform, then those things—not only when applied through fumigations, or eye-salves, or ointments, or potions, or any such methods, but even when they are suitably wrapped and bound together, or hung from the neck, or placed underneath in any other way, or approached by even the lightest touch—impress their power upon us. Therefore, these bindings, suspensions, wrappings, applications, and contacts are used for the conditions of the body and soul: in sickness, in health, in boldness, in fear, in sadness, in joy, and the like. They make the wearer graceful or terrible, accepted or rejected, honored and beloved, or hateful and abominable. For it is clear that passions of this kind are infused by the aforementioned means through art, no differently than in the grafting of trees, where the vital power is transferred from the trunk into the graft inserted into it.

### On rings and their compositions.

Rings also, which have always been held in high esteem, when they are fabricated at an opportune time, similarly bring forth virtue for us. Insofar as they affect the wearer, they can make one joyful or sad, gentle or fierce, bold or timid, lovable or hateful; they protect us against illnesses, poisons, demons, and against any other harmful things through these same powers. Now, the method of constructing rings is as follows:

->**The composition of rings.**<-

Namely, when some star ascends and is favorably aspected or conjoined with the Moon, it is necessary to take a stone subject to this star and to fashion a ring from a metal conforming to this star, and in it place the appropriate herb or root. Finally, one must engrave the names and characters, and furthermore not omit the proper fumigations <note>The practice of "feeding" the ring or talisman with the smoke of specific incense to complete the ritual.</note>. By the benefit of these rings, it is said he lived over one hundred and thirty years; and furthermore, he remained as vigorous as a young man...

### On fascination and its craft. CHAPTER L.

<margin>What fascination is.</margin> Fascination is a binding <note>original: "ligatio"; a magical constraint or spell</note> which proceeds from the spirit of the fascinator, entering through the eyes of the fascinated person and reaching into their very heart. <margin>The instrument of fascination: the spirit.</margin> The instrument of fascination is the spirit—namely, a certain pure, bright, and subtle vapor generated from the purest blood by the heat of the heart. This spirit constantly emits rays similar to itself through the eyes. These emitted rays carry the spiritual vapor with them, and that vapor carries blood with it. This is apparent in bleary <note>original: "lippis"; referring to ophthalmia or "pink eye," which was thought to be contagious through sight alone.</note> and red eyes, whose ray, emitted toward the eyes of a person looking at them, draws with it the vapor of corrupted blood, the contagion of which forces the eyes of the observer to suffer from a similar disease. 

Thus, an eye opened and directed toward someone with a strong imagination, using its rays like needles <margin>Rays: the vehicles of the spirit.</margin> (which are the vehicles of the spirit), darts them into the opposing eyes. This slow spirit, striking the eyes of the fascinated person, is incited by the heart of the "striker." Having claimed the chest as its own territory, it wounds the heart, and this foreign spirit infects the internal spirit. Hence, Apuleius says: "Those eyes of yours," he said, "having slipped through my eyes to the innermost depths of my chest, stir up a most piercing fire in my very marrow."

<margin>How fascination occurs.</margin> Know, therefore, that people are then most fascinated when, with a most frequent gaze, they direct the sharp edge of vision to another’s vision; they stare mutually into each other’s eyes, rays are joined to rays, and lights are joined to lights <note>original: "lumina luminibus"; "lumina" (lights) was a common poetic term for eyes.</note>. Whence the spirit and the amorous blood are thus wounded <note>original: "vulnerati"</note>, and they are carried toward the lover and the fascinator in no different a way than the blood and spirit of revenge, by some chance, fall upon the slayer. *For almost all generally fall toward the wound, and the blood*
*Spurts out toward that part where we are struck by the blow,*
*And if the enemy is at close quarters, the red fluid covers him.*

Such is the power of fascination, especially when the vapors of the eyes serve the emotion. Therefore, those who fascinate use eye-salves <term>collyria: medicinal washes or ointments for the eyes</term>, unguents, bindings, and the like, to affect and strengthen the spirit in this or that way. To induce love, they use eye-salves dedicated to Venus, made from *hippomanes* <term>hippomanes: a legendary substance found on the forehead of a newborn foal, or sometimes a plant, believed to be a potent aphrodisiac</term>, the blood of doves or sparrows, and similar things. To induce fear, they use eye-salves dedicated to Mars, such as those made from the eyes of wolves, hyenas, and the like. For calamity or sickness, they use those dedicated to Saturn. A similar reasoning must be held for each of these.

## On the divination of auspices.

There are certain other kinds of divination <note>original: "diuinationum genera"</note> depending on [natural] causes, which consist of various things: which 
sailors, for instance, use to forecast from probable signs:
many of these were handed down by Aristotle in his book on seasons. <note>Referring to "De temporibus," likely a reference to Aristotle's works on meteorology or natural history.</note>
Among these kinds of divination, auspices and auguries hold the 
primary place: which were once held in such high value among the Romans, <margin>The Romans did nothing without taking auspices.</margin>
that they performed nothing pertaining to public or private business 
without taking the auspices: indeed, the Etruscan <note>The Etruscans were the ancient neighbors of the Romans, famed for their complex rituals of divination.</note> people

on Divination. There are indeed several types of <margin>Types of auspices.</margin>
auspices: for some are called **pedestrian**, which 
evidently are taken from quadrupeds <note>four-footed animals</note>; some are **auguries**, which 
are taken from birds; some are **celestial**, which are from thunder and light-
ning; some are **falling** <note>original: "caduca"</note>, such as when something has fallen 
in a temple or elsewhere; some are **sacred**, which were taken from sacrifices. Of these 
certain ones were called **expiatory** <note>original: "piacula"</note> and **sad auspices**, such as when 
the victim had fled from the altar, or when struck had let out a lowing, 
or had fallen upon a different part of the body than was proper. 
To these is added **Exauguration** <note>A term for an omen indicating the withdrawal of divine favor</note>, as when for instance the staff <note>The "lituus," a curved wand used by augurs to mark out the sky.</note> 
had fallen from the hand of the one performing the augury, with which it was the custom to contemplate and 
take the auspice. Michael Scot <note>A famous 13th-century scholar and advisor to Frederick II, known for his works on astrology and the occult.</note> recites twelve <margin>Twelve kinds of auguries.</margin>
kinds of auguries, six indeed on the right, the names 
of which he says are: *fernoua, feruetus, confert, emponentem, sonna-
farnoua, sonnaferuetus*: and another six on the left, the 
names of which are: *confernoua, conferuetus, uiaram, herrenam,*

### CHAPTER LIV.
### On certain diverse living things, and other things: what significance they have in auguries.

The very first auspices <term>auspices: signs or omens, originally specifically those observed from birds</term> are to be taken at the very beginning of any work. For example, if at the start of a task you perceive your garment has been gnawed by moths <note>original: "a foricibus corrosum" — though 'forices' can refer to doors, in this context of 'corroded' garments, it refers to cloth-eating insects.</note>, cease from what you have begun. If, while going out, you stumble on the threshold, or strike your foot upon the road, cut short your journey. If any bad omen occurs to you at the start of your business, postpone what was started; do this lest your entire intention be frustrated or completed to no use. Instead, wait until you may seize a favorable hour for acting under a better omen. 

We see very many animals that, by a certain force implanted in them by nature, are wondrous <note>original: "praestigiosa"</note> and prophetic <note>original: "fatidica" — literally "fate-speaking."</note>. Does not the rooster most skillfully indicate the hours with his song, and put the lion to flight with open wings? Many birds foretell rain by their song and chattering; flies foretell it by their sharp stinging; and dolphins run before coming storms with their frequent leaps above the waters. It would be a long task to weave together again all the presages which the Phrygians, Cilicians, Arabs, Umbrians, Tuscans, and other peoples who followed auguries learned from birds and animals—omens which were proven by them through many experiments and examples. For in all things there are hidden...

BOOK ONE. 115

While the Crotoniates <note>Inhabitants of Croton, an ancient Greek city in Southern Italy known for its school of Pythagoras.</note> were fighting, an eagle [damaged] flying brought them victory. To Hiero <note>Hiero II, the King of Syracuse, whose rise to power was said to be marked by many such omens.</note> at the start of his [damaged], an eagle unexpectedly settling on his shield announced that he would be king in the future. At the birth of Alexander of Macedon, two eagles sitting atop his house all day portended the omen of a double empire over Asia and Europe for him. The same happened to Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, the son of Demaratus the Corinthian; while an exile from home due to sedition and traveling into Etruria seeking Rome, an eagle snatched his cap, flew high, and then placed it back upon his head, portending the Roman kingship for him. 

Now indeed, vultures also signify difficulty, harshness, and rapacity, which was verified by experience in the founding of the city <note>A reference to the contest between Romulus and Remus, where the sighting of vultures determined who should found Rome.</note>. They also show the locations of future slaughter, arriving seven days in advance; and because they look toward that side where the inferior party will be, as if gaping for a greater number of those to be killed, ancient kings were accustomed to send out scouts to report which way the vultures were turned. 

[Margin:] <margin>Auguries to be taken from the larger birds.</margin>

The Phoenix, however, promises the success of singular happiness; when it was seen, "New Rome" <note>Constantinople, established by Constantine the Great.</note> was founded under better auspices. The Pelican, because it risks itself for the sake of its children, signifies a man who will undergo danger through the devotion <note>original: "pietate"</note> of his friendship. The "painted bird" <note>original: "Picta auis"</note> gave its name to the city of the Pictavi <note>Modern-day Poitiers in France.</note> and prefigured the gentleness of the people by its color and voice. The Heron <note>original: "Ardea"</note> is an omen of arduous <note>original: "arduarum." Agrippa is using a common Renaissance pun linking the bird's name to the difficulty of an undertaking.</note> matters. The Stork, a bird of concord, brings about harmony. Cranes <note>original: "Grues"</note>—named from the ancient word *gruere*, as if to say *congruere* <note>meaning "to agree" or "to come together."</note>—always bring what is advantageous and cause one to beware the snares of enemies. The Hoopoe <note>original: "Cucupha"</note> indicates gratitude, for it alone returns thanks to its parents when they are worn out by old age. Conversely, the Hippopotamus, a parricide, announces ingratitude for favors and injustice. The Oryx-bird <note>original: "Origis auis." In ancient lore, the Oryx was often an antelope, but Agrippa here classifies it as a bird, possibly following a tradition of Egyptian hieroglyphic symbols where it represented envy.</note>, a most envious creature, signifies envy. 116 OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

[Margin:] <margin>Auguries which are taken from the smaller birds.</margin>

From the smaller birds: the talkative magpie announces guests. No bird flying past—if it turns from the left to the right—indicates joy; if it turns in the opposite direction, it indicates the opposite. The magpie <note>The Latin text here is slightly ambiguous but refers to the *pica* (magpie) or perhaps the *noctua* (little owl).</note> is very ill-omened, as is the little owl. Because the little owl unexpectedly attacks chicks just as death comes upon sight, it is believed to foretell death. However, because it is not blind in the darkness of night, it also signifies diligence and vigilance, as the spear of Minerva <note>original: "Mineronis haſta" (likely a typo for *Minervae*). The owl is the sacred bird of Minerva/Athena, the goddess of wisdom and war.</note> proved. 

The horned owl <note>Latin: *Bubo*. While the *noctua* is the little owl, the *bubo* is the larger eagle-owl, almost always seen as a terrifying omen in Roman culture.</note> was felt to be ill-omened by Dido <note>The tragic Queen of Carthage in Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note> regarding Aeneas. Concerning this bird, Virgil sang:

*And the solitary owl on the rooftops with a funereal song*
*Often complained and drew out long cries into a wail.* <note>original: "Solaq; culminibus ferali carmine bubo / Sæpe queri & longas in fletū ducere uoces." From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book IV.</note>

And Ovid wrote:
*The sluggish owl, a dire omen to mortals.* <note>original: "Ignauus bubo dirum mortalibus omen." From Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Book V.</note>

The same bird sang on the Capitol when Roman affairs were at a low point, and when the city of Fregellae <note>An ancient Volscian city that revolted against Rome in 125 BCE and was subsequently destroyed.</note> was demolished because of a conspiracy formed there. Almadel <note>A reference to the author of the *Ars Almadel*, a famous medieval grimoire or book of magic.</note> says that when owls and **Elicoraces** <note>This term likely refers to a specific type of crow or a magical name for a bird species used in the *Almadel* tradition.</note> come to dwell in unusual regions, it is a judgment upon the inhabitants of those regions and houses; this is because those birds delight in corpses and sense them beforehand, and men about to die are already, in a sense, corpses. 

But there is also the hawk, a herald of strife, of which it is said:
*We hate the hawk, because it always lives in arms.* <note>original: "Odimus accipitrem, quia uiuit ſemper in armis." From Ovid's *The Art of Love*.</note>

When Lælius, a legate of Pompey, was killed in Spain, a hawk flying over his head is said to have announced that fate. And Almadel says that birds of the same kind fighting among themselves signify a change in the kingdom. Truly, if birds of different species wage war against each other and meet where they are no longer seen, they portend a new battle for that region. Even the tiniest birds, by their arrival and their song, portend that a family will be increased or diminished.

The most marvelous kind of <term>augury</term><note>Augury is the ancient practice of divining the future or the will of the gods by observing the behavior of birds.</note>, however, is that by which some hear and understand the speech of animals; this is said to have been possible for Melampus, Tiresias, Thales, and <unclear>Apollonius</unclear> of Tyana, who is said to have excelled in the songs of birds. <meta>This page transitions from the observation of birds and animal behavior to the practice of extispicy—divination through the inspection of animal entrails, specifically the liver and heart.</meta>

Let Tages have invented those things.
<note>original: *Finxerit illa Tages.* Tages was a founding figure in Etruscan religion, a child-prophet who rose from a plowed furrow to teach the art of divination.</note>

Roman religion considered the liver to be the "head" or most important part of the internal organs. For this reason, when the <term>haruspices</term><note>Haruspices were specialized priests in ancient Rome who interpreted the will of the gods by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals, a practice known as haruspicy or extispicy.</note> were searching for the future within the entrails, they first inspected the liver. They identified two "heads" <note>Referring to the lobes of the liver.</note> within it; one they dedicated to the citizen and the other to the enemy. By comparing these heads, they would announce victory for one side or the other. We read an example of this in the poet Lucan, where the entrails signified the slaughter of Pompey's followers and the victory of Caesar's men in these verses:

        And what wickedness appeared in the entrails, not to go unpunished!
        Behold, he saw a mass of fibers growing upon the [first] head;
        The other head's part hangs sickly and withered,
        While the other part flashes and moves its veins with a wicked, swift pulse.
        <note>original: *Quodq; nefas nullis impune apparuit extis...* These lines are from Lucan's *Pharsalia* (1.617–622), an epic poem about the Roman Civil War. The "wicked pulse" of the liver was interpreted as a sign of Caesar’s impending, violent victory.</note>

Next, after the internal organs were fully examined, they sought the heart. If a sacrificial victim was found without a heart, or if the "head" was missing from the liver, these were considered death-bearing omens, and they were called "piacular" <note>from the Latin *piacularia*, meaning an omen requiring a specific ritual of atonement or expiation because it signaled a grave disturbance in the relationship with the gods.</note>. Similarly, it was a bad sign if the victim fled from the altar, or if it let out a lowing sound when struck, or if it fell on a part of the body other than what was proper. 

We read regarding these signs that on the day Julius Caesar first went out in purple robes and sat on a golden throne, the heart was twice found to be missing from the entrails while he was sacrificing. The liver was also missing from the entrails when Gaius Marius was sacrificing at Utica. The same occurred for the emperor Gaius <note>Gaius Caesar, better known as Caligula.</note> and for Marcus Marcellus. When the consuls Gaius Claudius and Lucius Petellius sacrificed victims, the liver suddenly rotted away; not long after, the former died of disease, and the latter fell by the weapons of the Ligurians...

It will be necessary to consider that very occurrence and what followed from it, and based on those results, to predict either the same or similar outcomes; for the same signs belong to the same events, and similar signs to similar events. Thus, portents preceded many excellent men and kings at their birth or death. 

As Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), a Roman statesman and philosopher who wrote *De Divinatione* (On Divination), a primary source for these stories.</note> relates regarding the boy Midas <note>The legendary King Midas, famous in myth for his "golden touch."</note>, ants dropped grains of wheat into his mouth while he was sleeping, which was an omen of great wealth. Likewise, when bees settled on the mouth of the infant Plato as he slept in his cradle, it was a prediction of the sweetness of his future eloquence. 

Hecuba, when she was about to give birth to Paris, dreamed that she gave birth to a burning torch that would set fire to Troy and all of Asia. The mother of Phalaris <note>Phalaris was the notorious tyrant of Akragas in Sicily, known for his cruelty and the "brazen bull."</note> dreamed she saw a statue of Mercury pouring blood onto the earth, which flooded the entire house. The mother of Dionysius <note>Dionysius I, the tyrant of Syracuse.</note> dreamed she gave birth to a little satyr; the actual event followed and confirmed these portentous dreams. 

The wife of Tarquinius Priscus <note>The fifth King of Rome; his wife Tanaquil was famously skilled in interpreting omens.</note>, seeing a flame lick the head of Servius Tullius <note>Servius Tullius was a slave in the royal household who eventually became the sixth King of Rome. The flame did not burn him, marking him as divinely chosen.</note>, predicted the kingship for him. In a similar way, after the fall of Troy, while Aeneas was debating with his father Anchises about their flight, a flame appeared licking the crown of Ascanius's head <note>Ascanius was the son of Aeneas and grandson of Anchises.</note>, causing him no injury. Since this portended a kingdom for Ascanius, it persuaded them to depart. 

All significant disasters have been preceded by portents and signs. Thus we read in the works of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> that during the consulship of Marcus Attilius and Gaius Portius, it rained milk and blood, which foretold that a powerful plague would invade Rome in the following year.

In a similar way, **Aeromancy** <term>Aeromancy: divination by observing atmospheric phenomena such as wind, clouds, or lightning.</term> provides prognostications through atmospheric impressions: by the blowing of winds, by rainbows, by halos, by mists and clouds, and by images perceived in the clouds and visions in the air.

Likewise, **Pyromancy** <term>Pyromancy: divination by fire or the behavior of flames.</term> is used for divining through fiery impressions: by comets <note>original: "stellas caudatas," literally "tailed stars."</note>, by fiery colors, and by visions and imaginings seen in the fire. To this category belong those signs mentioned by Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and author of the "Natural History."</note>: that earthly fires are perceived as messengers of storms when they appear pale and murmuring. Rain is also foretold if "mushrooms" <note>original: "fungi." This refers to carbon or soot buildup on a lamp wick, which was thought to predict rain.</note> appear in the lamps; if the flame flickers unsteadily, it portends wind. Also, when lamps extinguish their own flames or are difficult to light, it is a sign; likewise when sparks gather in clusters upon them, or when charcoal sticks to the bottom of pots when they are lifted, or when a contained fire casts out embers or emits sparks, or when ash crusts together on the hearth, and when charcoal glows intensely.

To these is joined **Capnomancy** <term>Capnomancy: from the Greek 'kapnos' (smoke); divination by observing the smoke from a sacrifice.</term>, so named from smoke, because it examines the flame and the smoke, as well as their colors, sounds, and movements: whether it rises straight up, is carried sideways, or rolls in a circle. > The blood-red peaks of the flames, and the fire born
> Through the air; she shows how the clear light of midday 
> Is scorned as the fire rises, then how it twists 
> Into the hollow likeness of a serpent...

Now, indeed, even in the craters of Etna and in the Nymphaean fields near Apollonia <note>An ancient Greek colony in modern-day Albania, famous for its "nymphaeum," a place where fire issued from the earth.</note>, auguries were taken from fire and flames. ### On the revival of the dead, on long-duration sleep, and on fasting. CHAPTER LVIII.

The Arabian philosophers agree that some men are able to raise themselves above the powers of the body and above the sensitive powers <term>sensitive powers: the faculties of the soul related to physical sensation and perception.</term>. Having overcome these through the perfection of the heavens and the Intelligences <term>Intelligences: celestial or angelic beings believed to govern the movements of the planets and stars.</term>, they receive a divine vigor into themselves. Since, therefore, the souls of all men are perpetual, and all spirits obey perfected souls, the Magi believe that perfected men can—through the powers of their own soul—restore other inferior souls (which have already become somewhat separated) to their dying bodies and breathe life into them again. 

This is not unlike how a dead weasel is said to be called back to life by the breath and voice of its parent, or how lions bring life to their stillborn offspring by breathing upon them <note>This refers to a common medieval bestiary myth where lion cubs were thought to be born dead and brought to life after three days by the father lion's breath.</note>. And since, as they say, all similar things applied to similar things result in similar natures, and everything that is passive and receives the action of an agent takes on the nature of that agent, they believe that certain herbs and magical preparations contribute significantly to this revival. 

Tradition says such preparations are made from the ashes of the Phoenix <note>A mythical bird that regenerates from its own ashes.</note> and from the shed skins <note>original: "exuuijs."</note> of serpents. While this might seem like a mere fable to most, and even impossible to many, it would only be so if it were not proven by historical evidence. For we read of many people who were drowned in water, others cast into fires or placed upon the funeral pyre, others killed in war, and others rendered lifeless by various means, who nonetheless returned to life even after several days.

### On divination which occurs through dreams. CAP. LIX.

THERE is also a species of divination which occurs during sleep—namely, of dreams—and it is proven by the traditions of philosophers, the authority of theologians, the examples of histories, and daily experience. However, I speak here of a **dream**, not of a **phantom** <note>original: "phantasma"</note> or a **non-prophetic dream** <term>insomnium</term> <note>Agrippa follows the classification of Macrobius, where "insomnium" refers to meaningless dreams caused by physical distress or daily anxieties, rather than divine messages.</note>; for these are vain and contain nothing of divination, but are born from the remnants of waking thoughts or the disturbance of the body. For whenever we are burdened by the comforts or discomforts of the body or fortune, then whatever kind of thought fatigued the mind while awake introduces itself to the sleeper—or sometimes its opposite.

For this reason, the same common rule for interpreting <unclear>dreams</unclear> cannot be applied to everyone; but rather, according to the [ancient] opinion, when the circumstances are the same as the things, [we assign] the same to the same, and similar things to similar ones. Thus, he who sees himself in the same or a similar vision shall designate for himself the same or a similar meaning, passion, fortune, action, or final outcome. Just as **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE). One must proceed in a similar way regarding dreams. 

Wherefore **Synesius** <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 CE), a Neoplatonist philosopher and bishop who wrote a famous treatise on dreams, encouraging people to keep "night-books" or dream journals.</note> commands that everyone should observe their own dreams and their subsequent outcomes—namely, what visions resulted in what kinds of events—and to commit these rules (that is, the visions and the occurrences) both in dreams and in waking to the memory. By a certain diligent observation of this kind, one accumulates many rules within oneself. From this accumulation, indeed, a certain art of divination and of interpreting one's own dreams gradually arises, provided that nothing slips from the memory. 

Moreover, dreams are more effective when the **Moon** occupies that sign which was in the ninth house of the **root of the nativity** <term>radicis nativitatis</term> <note>The birth chart or "horoscope" of an individual's moment of birth.</note>, or of the revolution of that year, or in the ninth sign from the sign of the profection <note>A method of traditional astrology used to determine which planetary themes are active in a given year.</note>. However, the truest and most certain divination comes neither by nature nor by human arts, but proceeds from **purified minds**.

### On the passions of the soul, and their origin, variety, and types. CHAPTER LXII.

The passions of the soul are nothing other than certain movements or inclinations arising from the apprehension <note>In Renaissance philosophy, *apprehensio* refers to the way the mind "grasps" or perceives an object before judging it.</note> of some thing, whether as good or evil, suitable or unsuitable. Now, perceptions of this kind are threefold: namely sensory, rational, and mental. Consequently, there are threefold passions in the soul: for sometimes they follow sensory perception, and then they regard a temporal good or evil, in the sense of convenience or inconvenience, pleasure or offense; these are called natural or animal passions. At other times they follow rational perception, and thus they regard good or evil in the sense of virtue and vice, praise and blame, the useful and the useless...

For the concupiscible power regards good and evil absolutely: and thus is caused love <note>original: "amor seu libido"</note> and, conversely, hatred. Or it regards the good as something absent, which causes cupidity or desire; and it regards evil as absent but imminent, which causes horror, flight, and abomination. Or it regards good and evil as present and attained: and thus from the former arises delight, joy, and pleasure; while from the latter arises sadness, anguish, and pain. 

The irascible power, however, regards good and evil under the aspect of difficulty—whether in attaining and obtaining it, or in fleeing and repelling it. This happens sometimes with confidence: and thus is caused hope on one hand, and true boldness on the other. Sometimes it happens with a lack of confidence, and thus arises desperation and fear or dread. Sometimes this irascible power rises up for vengeance, and this occurs only concerning a past evil—as in an injury or harm already inflicted—and this causes anger.

And so we find eleven passions in the soul itself, which are: **love, hatred, desire, horror, joy, pain, hope, despair, boldness, fear,** and **anger.**

Thus the magnet attracts iron, because in the order of the <term>Celestial Bear: the constellation Ursa Major, which was historically believed to govern magnetic forces</term> it holds a superior rank. Thus the diamond hinders the magnet, because in the <term>Martial order: the hierarchy of things governed by the planet Mars</term> it is superior to it. 

In a similar way, any man—through the intense emotions of his mind and also through the skillful application of the natures of things, being opportunely exposed to celestial gifts—if he has become stronger in solar virtue, he binds and draws the <unclear>inferior</unclear> into admiration and obedience. In the <unclear>Lunar</unclear> order, he draws them to servitude or weakness; in the <unclear>Saturnine</unclear> to <unclear>rest</unclear> or sadness; in the Jovial to the showing of veneration; in the Martial to fear or discord; in the Venusian to love or joy; in the Mercurial to persuasion and compliance, and similar states. <margin>The root of binding.</margin> Indeed, the root of such "binding" is the vehement and extreme affection of the soul itself, coinciding with the alignment of the celestial order. ### On speech and the virtues of words. CHAPTER [70]

Deep secrets and sacraments are inherent in those characters and in their figures, numbers, position, order, and revolution, so that Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD), an early Christian scholar who argued that names of power (like those of God or angels) lose their efficacy if translated from their original tongue.</note> therefore thinks that those names, when translated into another language, retain very little of their proper power, because they do not retain their natural significance. For only primary names—those which were rightly imposed because they signify naturally—possess natural activity. It is not so with those names which signify by convention <note>original: "ad placitum"; a philosophical term meaning names chosen by human agreement rather than reflecting the thing's true nature.</note>, which do not have activity as signifiers, but are merely certain natural objects in themselves. 

If there is any first, causal language, whose words have a natural significance, it is established to be Hebrew. He who holds the order of this language deeply and radically, and knows how to revolve its letters proportionately, will have the perfectly found norm and rule of any language. There are therefore twenty-two letters, which are the foundation of the world and of all creatures which are named in it; and every word and every creature exists through them, and from their revolutions they obtain their name, being, and form. 

It behooves the investigator of these letters to run through the individual combinations of letters for so long until the voice of God is revealed, and the text of the most sacred scriptures offers itself openly. For hence voices and words have efficacy in magical operations, because that in which nature first exercises its greatest power is the voice of God. But these matters belong to a higher level of speculation than should be treated in this book. Let us return to the division of the letters. Of these among the Hebrews, there are three "Mothers," namely: **אמש** <note>These are the Hebrew letters Aleph, Mem, and Shin. Hermann von Wied, Prince-elector [unclear] Duke of Westphalia and Angria, [unclear] Archbishop of Cologne and Paderborn, his most gracious Lord, Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim sends greetings.

BEHOLD NOW (most illustrious Prince and most ample prelate) the remaining books of <term>occult philosophy</term> <note>The study of hidden laws of nature, including astrology, alchemy, and natural magic.</note> or magic, which I recently promised to your Greatness I would publish when I released the first of them. However, the sudden and almost unexpected death of my princess, the Divine Margaret of Austria <note>Margaret of Austria (1480–1530) was the Governor of the Habsburg Netherlands and a major patron of Agrippa.</note>, occurring shortly thereafter, delayed my eagerness for publishing at that time.

Subsequently, the wickedness of certain "beaked" sycophants <note>original: "rostratorū sycophātarū." They have fought against me with a bitter continuation of hatred, envy, spite, and slanders. Some of these men, with raised eyebrows and puffed-out cheeks, denounced me for impiety with declaiming voices in the churches before the common people. Others filled the ears of the ignorant in every neighborhood with whispers in corners, spreading my infamy from house to house. Still others, in public and private assemblies, incited the Bishops, the princes, and even the Emperor himself against me.

Because of this, I began to hesitate whether I should publish these remaining books at all, as I suspected that by doing so I would expose myself to even greater slanders—tossing myself, as they say, out of the smoke and into the flame. A certain "rustic fear" <note>An idiom for a simple or perhaps unrefined hesitation.</note> came over me, lest by publishing them I might appear more troublesome than dutiful to you, and might even stir up the envy of those <term>Zoili</term> <note>Cynical or spiteful critics, named after Zoilus, a Greek grammarian known for his harsh criticism of Homer.</note> against your own Highness, exposing you likewise to the tongues of detractors. While all these things disturbed me with various forms of despair, I entrusted my hesitation to your own understanding...

## BOOK TWO.

### On the necessity of Mathematical disciplines, and on many wondrous works which are performed by mathematical arts alone. CHAPTER I.

**MATHEMATICAL** disciplines are so necessary and related to magic that anyone who [pursues] this without [them] <note>Agrippa argues that magic is a rigorous science; without the precision of mathematics, a practitioner is merely guessing.</note> wanders entirely from the path, [labors in vain], and by no means achieves the desired effect. For whatever [exists] in these lower natural powers <note>original: "virtutibus." In Renaissance science, a "virtue" is the specific hidden power or property of an object, like a magnet's power to pull iron.</note> is [ordered] by number, weight, measure, harmony, motion, and [arrangement]. All things that we see in the [lower world] have their root and foundation in these [mathematical principles].

Indeed, even without using natural powers, works similar to nature [can be created] through mathematical disciplines alone. As Plato says, these are things not truly partaking [in reality], but certain likenesses [imitating] bodies that walk or speak, yet they lack vital power <note>original: "virtute animali." This refers to the *anima* or soul-force that makes a creature alive, as opposed to a mere mechanical puppet.</note>. Such were the statues of Daedalus among the ancients, which were called self-moving machines <note>original: "αὐτόματα" (automata)</note>. Aristotle also mentions the tripods of Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and smithing, known as Hephaestus in Greek myth.</note> and Daedalus that moved themselves, which Homer relates came forward to the contest of their own accord—and which I have read...

<summary>This page introduces Book Two, arguing that mathematics is the essential foundation for magic because all natural things are governed by number and proportion. Agrippa describes how mathematical arts can even create "automata"—lifelike machines that mimic living beings without possessing a soul.</summary>

### On numbers, and their power and virtue. CHAP. II.

Severinus Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works on arithmetic and music were foundational for medieval education.</note> says: "All things whatsoever that have been constructed by the primeval nature of things seem to be formed by the ratio of numbers." For this was the principal model in the mind of the Creator. From this the multitude of elements is transformed; from this the cycles of the seasons; from this the motion of the stars and the revolution of the heavens; and the stability of all things exists through the binding of numbers.

...all things have great power and are most effective for obtaining **spirit-given** <note>original: "dæmonica." These are specifically suited to magical works, existing as a middle ground between the two <note>Referring to the "extremes" of the purely material and the purely intellectual or spiritual realms.</note>, adapted by a leaning toward the extremes, just as in the use of letters. ### Of Unity and its Scale. CHAPTER IV

Now let us determine specifically about the numbers themselves: because since number is nothing else than the repetition of unity, let us first consider unity itself. Unity penetrates every number most simply; it is the common measure, source, and origin of all numbers; it contains every number uniquely joined within itself, devoid of all multitude, always the same and immutable: hence even when multiplied by itself, it produces nothing but itself: it is indivisible and lacking all parts: but if it should ever be forced to be divided, it is not cut but multiplied, namely into unities. However, none of these unities is greater or less than the whole, in the way that a part is smaller than the whole: it is multiplied not into parts, but into itself. 

<margin>Names of Unity.</margin> For this reason, some have called this **concord**, others **piety**, others **friendship**, because it is repeated so that it is not cut into parts: but even **Martianus** <note>Martianus Capella, a 5th-century author whose work "The Marriage of Philology and Mercury" was a standard textbook on the liberal arts.</note> following the opinion of **Aristotle**, asserts it is named **Cupid** <note>original: "Cupidinem"</note>, for the reason that it is one alone, and wishes always to seek itself, and has nothing beyond itself; but being devoid of all pride or coupling, it turns back its fires into its own self. One, therefore, is the principle and end of all things, having neither principle nor end itself: nothing is prior to one, nothing is posterior to one. One is the true principle, and all things exist because of one, and...

## Concerning the number six and its scale.

The number six is the number of nature’s perfection within the whole sequence of numbers up to ten. It alone is so perfect that it results from the sum of its own parts, being neither excessive in abundance nor lacking in any way. For if you take its parts—namely, the sixth <note>1</note>, the third <note>2</note>, and the half <note>3</note>—and gather them together, they perfectly recreate the whole body of the number six <note>In mathematics, a "perfect number" is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its proper divisors.</note>. All other numbers lack this same perfection. This number is also thoroughly suited for generation and marriage, and is called the "seal of the world." 

For by the number six, the world was finished and perfected by God. On the sixth day, God saw all the things He had made, and they were very good <note>original: "valde bona"; a reference to Genesis 1:31.</note>. Therefore, the heavens, the earth, and all their host were perfected. It is also called the number of man, because man was created on the sixth day. Furthermore, it is called the number of redemption, because on the sixth day Christ suffered for our salvation; hence, the number has a great affinity with the Cross. 

It is also called the number of labor and servitude. For this reason, it was commanded in the Law <note>The Mosaic Law of the Old Testament.</note> that work should be done for six days; that manna should be collected for six days; that the earth should be sown for six years; and that a Hebrew servant should serve his master for six years. For six days the glory of the Lord rested upon Mount Sinai, covering it with a cloud. 

There are six wings on the cherubim <note>Agrippa refers here to the celestial beings described in the visions of Isaiah and Ezekiel; specifically, the Seraphim are described as having six wings.</note>. There are six circles in the firmament: the Arctic, the Antarctic, the two Tropics, the Equinoctial, and the Ecliptic. There are six wandering planets—Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon—which travel across the width of the Zodiac, moving back and forth across the ecliptic <note>Agrippa lists six here, setting the Sun apart as the central, stabilizing force of the heavens.</note>. There are six substantial qualities in the elements...

# On the septenary and its scale. CHAPTER 10.

The **number seven** <term>Septenary; the number seven</term> is of varied and manifold power. It consists of one and six, or of two and five, or of three and four; and it possesses unity as if it were a link between a **twin trinity** <note>This refers to the structure 3 + 1 + 3, where the number one serves as the central bridge between two groups of three.</note>. For this reason, if we consider its individual members and their joints, we must undoubtedly admit that it is most full of all majesty, both by the binding together of its parts and by its own individual fullness.

The Pythagoreans call it the **vehicle of human life**, for it does not borrow its power from its parts as much as it perfects by its own right of totality. Indeed, it encompasses the **body and the soul**: for the body consists of the four elements and is affected by the four qualities; meanwhile, the number three relates to the soul because of its threefold power—namely, the **rational**, the **irascible** <note>original: "irascibilem"; the "spirited" or "emotional" part of the soul associated with courage or anger.</note>, and the **concupiscible** <note>original: "concupiscibilem"; the "desiring" part of the soul associated with physical needs and appetites.</note>.

The number seven, therefore, because it consists of three and four, joins the soul to the body. The power of this number also pertains to the **generation of men**, for it causes a human being to be conceived, formed, brought forth, nourished, and to live, and it governs the entire constitution. For once the genital seed is received in the woman's womb, if it remains there for **seven hours** without being expelled, it is certain that life has taken hold. Then, in the **first seven days**, it coagulates and becomes fit to receive the human shape. Subsequently, it produces mature infants who are called *septimestres* <note>original Latin: "septimestres"; those born in the seventh month.</note>, that is, those born in the **seventh month**.

After birth, the **seventh hour** determines whether the infant will live; for it is understood that whoever sustains the breath of air beyond this number is born for life. After **seven days**, the infant sheds the remains of the umbilical cord. After **twice seven days**, its vision begins to move toward the light. In the **third seven-day period** (twenty-one days), it now freely turns its eyes and its entire face. After **seven months**, the teeth begin to emerge. After the **second seven-month period** (fourteen months),

213 OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

-># Concerning the Number Eight and its Scale<-

The Pythagoreans call the number eight the number of **justice** and **fullness**. First, they call it so because it is divided into "evenly even" numbers <note>original: *pariter pares*. In Pythagorean mathematics, this refers to a number that can be divided by two repeatedly down to unity (8 halved is 4, 4 halved is 2, 2 halved is 1).</note>; indeed, this very vision of it being twice-doubled in the same ratio is why the name of "justice" became associated with it, due to this equality of division. Secondly, it received the name of "fullness" because of the structure of bodily solidity, for it is the first number to produce a solid body <note>As the first cube (2³), eight represents three-dimensional depth and physical reality.</note>.

Hence comes the custom of **Orpheus** <note>A legendary Greek hero and musician whose "Orphic Hymns" were central to Renaissance magic.</note> swearing by eight deities whenever he wished to appeal to divine justice. Their names are: **Fire**, **Water**, **Earth**, **Heaven**, **Moon**, **Sun**, **Phanes** <note>In Orphic myth, the primeval deity of light and generation.</note>, and **Night**. There are also exactly eight visible spheres of the heavens. The property of physical nature is signified to us through this number, which Orpheus encompassed in his maritime hymn of the eight <note>Refers to the *Hymn to the Sea*, which Agrippa interprets as relating to the octonary structure of the elements.</note>.

This is also called the number of the **covenant** and **circumcision**, which was commanded to be performed for the Jews on the eighth day. There were also eight ornaments of the priest in the Old Law: namely, the **linen breeches**, the **tunic**, the **girdle**, the **miter** <note>original: *tyara*.</note>, the **long robe** <note>original: *stola talaris*.</note>, the **ephod** <note>original: *perhumerale*, the shoulder-garment of the High Priest.</note>, the **breastplate of judgment** <note>original: *rationale*, the garment containing the Urim and Thummim.</note>, and the **golden plate**.

This number also pertains to **eternity** and the **consummation of the world**, as it follows the number seven, which is the symbol of time. For this reason, it is also the number of **beatitude**; for Christ teaches just so many degrees of blessedness in the Gospel of Matthew <note>The eight Beatitudes from the Sermon on the Mount.</note>. It is also called the number of **salvation** and **preservation**, for just so many souls were made safe in Noah's Ark from the deluge of waters.

Furthermore, there were eight sons of Jesse, of whom **David** was the eighth. Likewise, **Zacharias**, the father of John, regained his speech on the eighth day. They claim this is the number of **Dionysus**, who was brought into the light in the eighth month; in eternal testimony of this, the island of Naxos was dedicated to him and obtained this privilege: that only the women of Naxos might give birth easily in the eighth month.

<summary>This page explores the mystical significance of the number eight, defining it as the number of justice, physical solidity, and salvation. It draws parallels between Pythagorean math, Orphic hymns, Jewish priestly vestments, and Christian concepts of eternity and the Beatitudes.</summary>

<keywords>Eight, Octonary, Justice, Pythagoras, Orpheus, Solid Body, Circumcision, Priestly Ornaments, Beatitudes, Noah's Ark, Dionysus, Naxos</keywords>

->## On the Number Nine, and its Scale.<-
### CHAPTER XII.

The number nine is sacred to the **Muses** <note>In Greek mythology, the nine Muses were the goddesses of the arts and sciences, daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne (Memory).</note>, and <unclear>it is joined</unclear> to the orders of divine spirits. There are nine moving spheres, and according to those there are nine <unclear>Muses</unclear>, namely: Calliope, Urania, Polyhymnia, Terpsichore, Melpomene, Erato, Euterpe, and Thalia. Indeed, these nine Muses are assigned to the nine spheres in such a way that the first represents the highest sphere, which they call the **First Mover** <note>original: *primum mobile*; in the geocentric model of the universe, this was the outermost sphere that moved all the inner ones.</note>, and so on, descending step-by-step according to the written order until the last, which represents the sphere of the Moon. It follows this arrangement: 

*   **Calliope** is assigned to the **First Mover**.
*   **Urania** to the **starry heaven** <note>The sphere of the "fixed stars," or the zodiac.</note>.
*   **Polyhymnia** to **Saturn**.
*   **Terpsichore** to **Jupiter**.
*   **Clio** <note>Agrippa lists Clio here, though she was missing from the initial list of names in the transcription.</note> to **Mars**.
*   **Melpomene** to the **Sun**.
*   **Erato** to **Venus**.
*   **Euterpe** to **Mercury**.
*   **Thalia** to the **Moon**.

There are also nine orders of blessed angels, namely: **Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominations, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Archangels, and Angels**. These are symbolized by the nine stones mentioned by the prophet Ezekiel: sapphire, emerald, carbuncle, beryl, onyx, chrysolite, jasper, topaz, and sardius <note>Referencing Ezekiel 28:13, where these precious stones are listed in the description of the "King of Tyre" or the "Anointed Cherub" in Eden.</note>. This number also contains a great and hidden **mystery** <note>original: *sacramentum*</note> of the **Cross**; for at the **ninth hour** <note>According to the Gospels, Jesus died at the ninth hour of the day (roughly 3:00 PM).</note>, our Lord Jesus Christ gave up his spirit. 

Furthermore, the ancients used to bury the dead on the ninth day, and it is said that **Minos** <note>The legendary first King of Crete and a judge of the underworld.</note> received laws from **Jove** <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note> in a cave every nine years. For this reason, this number was particularly observed by **Homer**, whether in the establishing of laws, the giving of oracles, or when a plague was about to rage. **Astrologers** also observe **enneatic years** <term>Enneatic years: cycles of nine years</term> in the ages of men, just as they do with the varied cycles they call **climacterics** <note>Agrippa refers to "climacteric years," which were believed to be critical or dangerous years in a person's life, usually occurring in multiples of seven or nine.</note>, which are marked by significant changes. Sometimes, however, it carries a note of both perfection and incompleteness, because it <insert>reaches toward</insert> the **denary** <note>The number ten, which was considered the perfect "container" of all numbers.</note>...

### XIII. [The Number Ten and its Scale]

...or universal, <note>The number ten is often called "the universe" in Pythagorean thought because it contains all the numerical patterns that follow it.</note> the full curriculum of life: for beyond it, numbers are not counted except by repetition. It either folds all numbers within itself or unfolds them through itself and its own parts by multiplication. For this reason, it is considered to have a manifold religious significance and power, and is well-suited for purifying the soul. Hence the ancients spoke of "denary ceremonies," <note>original: *ceremonias denarias*; rituals based on the number ten.</note> in which those who were to be purified or about to undergo sacred rites were required to abstain from certain things for ten continuous days.

This was why among the Egyptians, it was the custom that anyone wishing to be initiated into the sacred rites of Isis would usually be ordered to fast for ten days. Apuleius testifies to this regarding himself, saying: <note>This quote is from Apuleius’s *Metamorphoses* (The Golden Ass), Book XI, describing his initiation into the mysteries of Isis.</note> "He clearly commanded, in the presence of all the witnesses, that for those ten continuous days I should restrain the pleasures of food; I was to eat no animal, and I was to be without wine." <note>original: *Illud plane cunctis arbitris præcepit, decem illis continuis diebus cibariam uoluptatem coërcerem, & neq; ullum animal eſſem, & inuinius eſſem.*</note>

There are ten parts of the sanguine man: <note>original: *sanguinei hominis*; referring to the physical, living human composed of blood and spirit.</note> the menstrual fluid, the sperm, the formative spirit, the mass <note>likely referring to the unformed embryo or "mola."</note>, the humors, the organic body, the vegetative faculty, the sensitive faculty, reason, and the mind. 

There are also ten simple integral parts constituting a human: bone, cartilage, nerve, tendon, <note>original: *chorda*.</note> ligament, artery, vein, membrane, <note>original: *panniculus*.</note> flesh, and skin. 

There are also ten limbs <note>original: *artus*.</note> of which the internal man consists: the spirit, the brain, the lungs, the heart, the liver, the gall, the spleen, the kidneys, the genitals, and the womb. <note>original: *matrix*.</note>

Furthermore, there were ten curtains in the Temple, ten strings on the psaltery, and ten musical instruments with which the psalms were sung, whose names are:
*   **Neza**, <note>Hebrew: *Netzach* (Victory/Eternity).</note> in which odes were sung.
*   **Nablum**, <note>Hebrew: *Nevel*.</note> the same as an organ [or lute].
*   **Mizmor**, <note>Hebrew: *Mizmor*.</note> in which psalms [were sung].
*   **Sir**, <note>Hebrew: *Shir*.</note> in which songs [were sung].
*   **Tephila**, <note>Hebrew: *Tefillah*.</note> in which prayers [were sung].
*   **Beracha**, <note>Hebrew: *Berakhah*.</note> in which blessings [were sung].
*   **Halel**, <note>Hebrew: *Hallel*.</note> in which praises [were sung].
*   **Hodaia**, <note>Hebrew: *Hodaya*.</note> in which thanksgivings [were sung].
*   **Ajre**, <note>Hebrew: *Ashrei* (Happy/Blessed).</note> in which someone's happiness <note>original: *felicitas*.</note> [was sung].

222 ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

...neither an attraction, nor a ladder leading to higher things: nor does it possess any merit, yet sometimes it receives free grace from God, like he who was called to the Lord’s vineyard at the eleventh hour, and received the same reward as those who bore the burden and heat of the day. <note>A reference to the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard from Matthew 20:1-16.</note>

However, the number twelve is divine, and is that by which celestial things are measured; for it is an aid to the dominion of the celestial signs and spirits. For there are twelve signs in the zodiac, over which twelve principal angels preside, supported by the outpourings <note>original: "irrigationibus"</note> of the great name of God. Jupiter completes its course in twelve years, and the Moon traverses twelve degrees every day. 

In the human body, there are twelve principal joints, namely: in the hands <note>the wrists</note>, elbows, shoulders, hips, knees, and the ankles <note>original: "vertebris pedum," literally "the vertebrae of the feet"</note>. Furthermore, there is great power in the number twelve within divine mysteries. God chose the twelve-fold family of Israel and set twelve princes over them; just as many stones were placed in the depths of the Jordan, and He commanded the same number to be fixed upon the breastplate of the priest. There were also twelve loaves of showbread <note>original: "panes facierum," literally "bread of the faces"</note>, and the altar was constructed from just as many stones; the "bronze sea" built by Solomon was supported by the same number of lions <note>The biblical description in 1 Kings 7:23-25 describes twelve oxen; Agrippa here writes "leones" (lions), possibly conflating the sea with Solomon's throne.</note>. There were just as many fountains in Elim, just as many spies sent to the land of promise, and just as many apostles of Christ set over the twelve tribes. 

Twelve thousand are numbered among the sealed people, and of the [heavenly] <note>damaged text: "coeli"</note>; the Queen of Heaven is crowned with twelve stars; and in the Gospel, twelve baskets are filled with the fragments of the multiplying loaves; twelve angels preside over the twelve [gates] <note>damaged text: "portis"</note> of the city, and there are twelve stones of the celestial Jerusalem. 

In the lower realms, many growing things also proceed by this number: thus the hare and the rabbit, being most fertile, conceive and give birth twelve times a year; the female camel carries her young for just as many months; and the peacock lays twelve eggs.

226 OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY
->### On the power and virtues of numbers which are above the Twelve. ###<-
->### CHAPTER XIII. ###<-

The remaining numbers beyond twelve are likewise adorned with various effects, the power and virtues of which must be understood from their origin and their component parts, insofar as they are constituted from various groupings of simple numbers or by the effect of multiplication. Sometimes their signified perfection results from the subtraction or the surpassing of the preceding number; furthermore, they contain within themselves the sacred mysteries of certain secrets. 

Thus, the **thirteenth** number indicates the mystery of Christ’s appearance to the Gentiles <note>The Epiphany.</note>; for on the thirteenth day after his birth <note>original: "natalem diem"</note>, he was manifested to the Magi. The **fourteenth** number also bears the figure of Christ, who was sacrificed on the fourteenth moon of the first month; on which day the children of Israel were commanded to celebrate the <term>Passover <note>original: "Phase," from the Hebrew 'Pesach,' meaning "to pass over."</note></term> to the Lord, which is to say, the transition. Matthew observes this number so carefully that, in order to maintain it everywhere in the generations of Christ, he omitted some generations <note>A reference to the genealogy in Matthew 1:1-17, which is structured into three sets of fourteen generations.</note>. 

The **XV.** [15th] number is a symbol of spiritual ascents, and therefore the Song of Ascents <note>original: "canticum graduum," referring to Psalms 120–134.</note> is adapted to it in fifteen steps. To this number are also assigned the fifteen years added to the life of King **Hezekiah**; and the fifteenth day of the seventh month is held as venerable and holy <note>The start of the Feast of Tabernacles or Sukkot.</note>. 

The **XVI.** [16th] number, being composed of an equilateral square <note>4x4=16</note> and the "parent of the ten" <note>The "parent of the ten" refers to the quaternary (4), because 1+2+3+4=10. This was a core Pythagorean concept.</note>, is for that reason called the "number of happiness" by the **Pythagoreans**. It also encompasses all the prophets of the Old Testament, as well as the apostles and evangelists of the New Testament <note>Agrippa likely counts 16 here by totaling the 4 major/12 minor prophets, or the 12 apostles plus the 4 evangelists.</note>.

### Concerning the signs of numbers, established in certain gestures. CHAPTER XVI.
