## CHAPTER THREE.
### On the origin of this power of the King regarding sacred matters.

[Marginalia:]
<margin>Cyprian.</margin>
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
<margin>Tertullian.</margin>
<margin>Aug.</margin>
<margin>Justinian.</margin>
<margin>Authors of the opposing opinion.</margin>
<margin>Bellarmine.</margin>
<margin>Becanus.</margin>
<margin>Suarez.</margin>

SINCE there is indeed great dispute regarding the origin of this power, it will be worthwhile to explain more fully the steps by which one arrives at this conclusion. There is no one who does not know that all power is from God: but how it comes to Kings in sacred matters is what is debated.

First, therefore, it must be established that this power was bestowed upon kings by the very creation and institution of the royal dignity. For when God instituted kingdoms, He gave Kings the right to command in all things which are necessary for the salvation of the people. And religion is the most necessary of all. Therefore, they also received the right to command in it. This was the view of Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage and an early Christian writer.</note>, when he says that God is the author of **both swords** <note>original: "vtriusque gladii"; the "two swords" theory refers to the division of spiritual and temporal power.</note>: and of Augustine, who teaches that Kings serve God in this, that in their kingdom they command good things, pertaining not only to human society, but also to divine religion.

Secondly, this power is confirmed by positive divine law. In the Old Testament, God commanded the King in explicit words to write out for himself a copy of the law, and to read it all the days of his life, so that he might know how to keep what is written. This ought not to be understood only regarding private observance, but especially regarding public care. For the King is appointed guardian of the law not only for himself, but for the people. Tertullian says that the **King is second from God, and less than God alone**; which must be understood universally.

Thirdly, this same point is clear from the practice of the primitive Church and the decrees of the Emperors. Augustine writes that it pertains to the care of the Emperor to ensure that not only temporal peace, but also religion, flourishes in his kingdom. Thus we see the Emperors passed laws concerning baptism, the Eucharist, the punishment of heretics, and the life and conduct of the Clergy. Justinian <note>Justinian I (reigned 527–565 AD), the Byzantine Emperor known for his massive codification of Roman law.</note> in his *Constitutions* often professes that he has the highest care for the dogmas of religion and the integrity of the Priests.

From these things, it follows that this power is not something accidental or extraordinary, but is of the essence of royal dignity. For the King is like the soul in the body of the commonwealth: just as the soul spreads itself through all members and cares for all, so the King cares for all the affairs of his kingdom.

But against this truth, several have risen in our age who attempt to strip this power from Kings entirely. Principal among these are **Bellarmine**, **Becanus**, and **Suarez** <note>These were prominent Jesuit theologians who argued for the "indirect power" of the Pope over temporal rulers.</note>. Their opinion is that Kings possess no power in sacred matters, except insofar as it is delegated to them by the Church. For they say that the King is only a Christian, and as such is subject to the Pastors in spiritual matters. From this they infer that he cannot decide on religion, but must only execute what has been decreed by the Pope or a Council.

Bellarmine says that Royal power is only concerned with temporal matters and is ordained toward a bodily end; while Ecclesiastical power is concerned with spiritual matters and is ordained toward an eternal end. From this he concludes that these two powers are so distinct that the King has no right in sacred matters, except perhaps by way of defense and execution. Suarez likewise contends that this power was not given to the King by God, but is merely human and civil; while spiritual power is divine, and bestowed only upon the Apostles and their successors.

But these authors are in great error. For first, it is false that royal power is only concerned with temporal things. For it is concerned with men, who consist of soul and body: and the King ought to care for the whole man, not just a part. Furthermore, the end of royal power is not only earthly peace, but the happiness of the people, which cannot exist without religion. Therefore the King ought to direct all things to this end. Moreover, if the King did not have this power, he could not be the **guardian of both tables** <note>original: "custos vtriusque tabulæ"; referring to both the first table (duties to God) and second table (duties to neighbors) of the Ten Commandments.</note>, which nevertheless is attributed to him by God.

As for what they say, that the King is subject to the Pastors in spiritual matters: a distinction must be made between the **person** and the **office**. The person of the King, as a Christian, is subject to the Word of God and the Sacraments, which are dispensed by the Pastors. But the office of the King is not subject to the office of the Pastor: for both are from God immediately, and are supreme in their own order. Just as a Physician is subject to the King as a citizen, but not as a physician; so Pastors are subject to the King as subjects, but the King does not command them in those things which are purely sacramental. But in the external government and direction of religion, the King is above all, even above the Priests.

Finally, if this opinion were true, it would follow that the King is only a **lictor of the Church** <note>original: "lictorem Ecclesiæ"; a lictor was a Roman official who carried out the orders and punishments of a magistrate. The author argues the King is not merely the Church's "executioner" or servant.</note>: which is against royal dignity. For God placed Kings upon His throne so that they themselves might judge and rule, not so that they might be ministers of another’s will. Thus we rightly conclude that this power is given to Kings immediately by God, and is part of their supreme jurisdiction.

This, however, does not remove the distinction between the internal and external forum. In the **internal forum** <note>The "internal forum" usually refers to the realm of conscience and private confession.</note>, which is of conscience, the Pastors have their function; but in the **external forum** <note>The "external forum" refers to public administration, law, and visible governance.</note>, which is of government and judgment, the King is supreme. Neither does the King invade the Priestly function: for he does not teach, he does not baptize, he does not consecrate; but he ensures that all these things are done rightly and in order by the Priests. That is, he does not exercise sacred acts himself, but he commands that they be exercised, and he brings forth laws concerning them.

<summary>This page argues that a King's authority over religious matters is an inherent part of his divine office from creation, refuting Jesuit claims that kings are merely the secular enforcers of Church decrees.</summary>
<keywords>divine right of kings, royal supremacy, two swords, both tables of the law, internal and external forum, Bellarmine, Suarez, Justinian, governance</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Chapter Three, transitioning from the theoretical origin of royal power to a systematic rebuttal of the arguments posed by Cardinal Robert Bellarmine and other Catholic theologians who argued for the supremacy of the Church over the State.</meta>

18

[Marginalia:]
<margin>Bellarmine’s first reason.</margin>
<margin>That reason is proved.</margin>
<margin>Its confirmation.</margin>
<margin>Solution to the first reason.</margin>
<margin>Another solution.</margin>
<margin>Inconveniences that follow from that opinion.</margin>

NOW let us descend to a more accurate examination of the foundations laid by Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit Cardinal and one of the most important figures in the Counter-Reformation, known for defending papal authority.</note> and others. Their first reason is this: The power of the king is merely human, arising from the consent of men; however, spiritual power is divine, instituted by God alone. Therefore, human power cannot command divine power.

This reason rests on a false assumption. For royal power is not merely human, but divine, as has been proved before. For it is God who constitutes kings and who gives them the right to command. For although the choice of a person is sometimes made by men, the power itself is from God. Just as in marriage, the consent of the spouses makes the marriage, but the power of the husband itself is ordained by God.

Furthermore, even if it were granted that royal power were human, it would not follow that it could not be concerned with divine matters. For man himself was made by God to worship God, and human society is ordered toward this end. Therefore, the power that governs society ought to look toward this end. Otherwise, it would be inferior to its own purpose.

**The second reason:** The end of royal power is temporal—namely, peace and justice; the end of ecclesiastical power is eternal—namely, the salvation of souls. But temporal things ought to serve spiritual things. Therefore, the King ought to serve the Church.

I respond: a distinction of ends does not create a distinction of powers such that one is subjected to the other. For the Physician has the end of health, and the Farmer the end of food; yet these ends are different from the end of the King, and nonetheless the King is not subject to them, but they to the King. Moreover, it is false that the end of the King is only temporal. For the King is the **guardian of both tables** <note>original: "custos vtriusque tabulæ"; referring to the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, implying the King is responsible for enforcing both religious duties (the first table) and social morality (the second table).</note>, and he must take care that his subjects live piously and religiously, which pertains to the eternal end. Therefore, the King and the Pastor strive toward the same end, but by different ways: the King by the way of command and coercion, the Pastor by the way of persuasion and teaching.

**The third reason:** The King, as a Christian, is a son of the Church; but a son does not command his mother. Therefore, the King does not command the Church.

This reason is purely figurative. The King is a son of the Church by reason of grace and the doctrine by which he is nourished; but by reason of his office, he is the **Father of the Fatherland** <note>original: "Pater patriæ"</note> and the guardian of the Church. He does not command the Church insofar as it is a spiritual society of the faithful, but he commands ecclesiastical persons insofar as they are members of the republic, and he disposes of the external affairs of the Church for the common good. Just as a head of a household, though he may be the spiritual son of his Pastor, nevertheless commands him in his own house in those things which pertain to domestic discipline.

**The fourth reason:** Priests have the power of **binding and loosing** <note>original: "ligandi & soluendi"; a reference to the "Power of the Keys" granted to the Apostles in the New Testament to forgive or retain sins.</note>; the King does not have this. Therefore, Priests are above the King.

I respond: the power of binding and loosing is the power of the keys, which is in the **court of conscience** <note>original: "foro conscientiæ"; the internal spiritual realm.</note>; the power of the King is the power of the sword, which is in the **external court** <note>original: "foro externo"; the public legal realm.</note>. These two powers do not conflict. A King can be subject to the keys of the Priest, and yet the Priest be subject to the sword of the King. The former binds the soul through censures; the latter binds the body through laws and punishments.

**The fifth reason:** In the Old Testament, King Uzziah <note>original: "Ozias"; see 2 Chronicles 26, where the king was struck with leprosy for attempting to offer incense in the Temple.</note> was punished by God because he wanted to burn incense, which was a priestly duty. Therefore, Kings ought not to meddle in sacred matters.

I respond: the example of Uzziah does nothing against our opinion. For we do not say that the King ought to exercise priestly functions, such as sacrificing, administering sacraments, and the like; for these are proper to Priests. But we say that the King ought to command that these things be done, and punish those who do not act rightly. Uzziah sinned not because he commanded the Priests, but because he wanted to be a Priest himself. For a distinction must be made between the **right of commanding** and the **right of executing** <note>original: "ius imperandi & ius exequendi"</note>. The King has the right of commanding in all things, but not the right of executing everything by himself. Just as he does not practice the medical art, nor the craft of a smith, but nevertheless he commands doctors and smiths.

**The sixth reason:** The Apostles and the primitive Church governed sacred matters for three hundred years without Kings. Therefore, royal power is not necessary for governing sacred matters.

I respond: we do not ask what can be done by way of necessity, but what ought to be done according to the order instituted by God. At that time, there were no Christian Kings; therefore, the Church was forced to look out for itself, as if in an extraordinary state. But after Kings became Christian, they succeeded to that right which God had destined for them from the beginning. Just as a ward governs his own affairs through tutors until he reaches age, but then he himself assumes the controls. So the Church under Gentile Kings was as if under tutors; but under Christian Kings, it has its own proper defenders and rulers.

**The seventh reason:** If the King had this power, he could change religion at his whim, as some Kings of England have done.

I respond: an argument from abuse to the right itself is not valid. The King does not have the power to change religion, but to protect and preserve the true religion. If he does otherwise, he sins against God; but this does not take away his right, just as cruelty does not take away a King’s power in civil matters. It is always presupposed that the King ought to use his power according to the Word of God. If he does otherwise, one must obey God rather than men. But this does not cause the power itself to be transferred to another.

From all these things it is clear that the reasons of the adversaries are not of such great weight that they can undermine the truth already proved. It remains settled, therefore, that the King is supreme in his kingdom even in sacred matters, insofar as they pertain to external government and jurisdiction.

<summary>This page systematically refutes seven arguments by Cardinal Bellarmine against royal supremacy, distinguishing between the King's "right to command" religious order and the Priest's "right to execute" spiritual rituals.</summary>
<keywords>Robert Bellarmine, royal supremacy, two swords, power of the keys, court of conscience, King Uzziah, right of command vs execution, external government</keywords>

[Marginalia:]
<margin>First
reason.</margin>
<margin>Second
reason.</margin>
<margin>Third
reason.</margin>

<margin>Fifth

AFTER we have refuted the principal reasons of our adversaries, it remains for us to briefly gather together those things which follow from what has been said, and to clear up certain doubts.

First, it follows that there are not two bodies in the same commonwealth <note>original: "respublica"</note>, one spiritual and the other temporal, which are ruled by different heads; but that there is one single body, of which the King is the head under Christ. For two heads in the same body would be a monster. In a Christian kingdom, the Church and the Commonwealth are not two different things, but one and the same multitude of people, considered from different perspectives. As they are citizens, they are members of the commonwealth; as they are the faithful, they are members of the Church. Therefore, just as there is one people, so there ought to be one supreme power.

Secondly, it follows that the Pastors of the Church do not possess **coercive power** <term>coercive power: the legal authority to compel obedience through force or punishment</term>, except insofar as it is granted to them by the King. For their own power is purely spiritual, and consists in doctrine, admonition, and spiritual censures <note>such as excommunication</note>. If they should command anything external that has the force of law, they hold that from Royal authority. This is why it is said in law that Bishops have "ordinary jurisdiction" in those things which belong to the **external forum** <term>external forum: the realm of public, legal administration and visible church discipline, as opposed to the internal forum of private conscience</term>, but they do so under the King and by the law of the Realm.

Thirdly, it follows that the King can and ought to make laws concerning sacred matters: not indeed so that he may invent new dogmas, but so that he may cause those things which are commanded in the Word of God to be observed. He can, therefore, convoke Synods <note>assemblies of clergy</note>, preside over them, confirm their decisions, or even invalidate them if they act against law and right. He can also dispose of Church property, the persons of the Clergy, and all external discipline.

At this point, however, a doubt is raised: **Can the King judge in controversies of faith?** I answer: the King does not judge concerning faith by way of a "Dogmatic definition"—for that is the role of the Pastors gathered in a Synod—but he judges by way of jurisdiction and execution. That is, after a matter has been discussed by the Pastors, the King examines whether it has been defined according to the Scriptures; and if he finds it to be so, he sanctions and promulgates it by his own authority. But if the Pastors should err, the King ought to employ others, or seek the truth himself from the Word of God. For the King must not follow whatever the Priests say with blind obedience, but he must himself "render an account to God" for the religion of his kingdom.

Another doubt: **Are Priests subject to the King in spiritual matters?** I answer: if by "spiritual matters" you mean the sacred acts themselves, such as teaching and administering the sacraments; in these things the King does not command them what they *ought* to do, but rather sees to it that they *do* them according to the Word of God. But if you mean the governance of persons and external order, in these things they are certainly subjects. For a Priest, although he is a Priest, does not cease to be a subject.

A third doubt: **What if the King commands something against the faith or good morals?** I answer with the Apostle: *We must obey God rather than men* <note>original: "Deo magis obediendum est quàm hominibus"; See Acts 5:29</note>. In such a case, subjects ought not to obey, but they ought to suffer punishment rather than act against their conscience. It is not, however, permitted for them to take up arms against the King for that reason, or to depose him; rather, they must appease God with prayers and patience. For the power of the King is from God, and is to be judged by God alone.

From all these things it is clear that our doctrine is consistent with the Scriptures, the Church Fathers, and right reason. For we do not flatter Kings when we assert their right, nor do we do injury to Priests when we keep them within their own order. For both have their own parts, which do not obstruct each other, but rather bring help. For the King protects the Priesthood with his sword, while the Priesthood establishes the King’s throne with its prayers and doctrine.

Therefore, the peace of the Church and the Commonwealth flourishes most when these two powers conspire together in friendship, and each one keeps itself within its own limits. That this may happen, we must pray to God, who holds the hearts of Kings in His hand, that He may give them wisdom and zeal for His glory; and that He may give the Pastors a spirit of humility and truth, so that they do not grow proud in their **seat of authority** <note>original: "cathedra"; the bishop's chair</note>, but faithfully feed the flock of Christ.

These are the things which seemed necessary to say concerning this most grave question. If anyone weighs them rightly, he will easily see where the truth lies, and how far they wander from the right path who either subject Kings to the Pope, or exclude sacred matters from the care of Kings. We, however, persist in this opinion, which antiquity has approved, and which usage itself has proven to be most wholesome.

THE END.

<summary>This concluding page argues for a unified "body politic" under the King’s leadership, asserting that while clergy handle doctrine, the King holds ultimate jurisdiction over the Church's external administration. It balances royal authority with the principle of "passive obedience," arguing that subjects should suffer rather than rebel if a King's commands conflict with faith.</summary>

# PREFACE.

## TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND REVEREND
## LORD CLAUDE DE LA GUICHE,
## ARCHBISHOP OF SENS, PRIMATE OF THE GAULS
## AND GERMANY, AND MOST AMPLE COUNSELOR 
## TO THE KING.

**IF EVER BEFORE**, most illustrious Prelate, I thought that this most useful and likewise most difficult discipline <note>Bodin refers here to "political science" or the study of the Commonwealth.</note> should be handed down and explained, now certainly I am fully persuaded that it must seem almost necessary. This is because at this time, as the saying goes, we are all **brought back to this anvil** <note>original: "ad incudem hanc." A Latin idiom meaning to start over or to work laboriously on a difficult problem.</note>, since Republics are governed not so much by order and law as by whim and lust. Indeed, not only the minds of men but the very affairs of state seem inclined toward ruin, unless they are propped up by a certain divine spirit and the counsel of prudent men. For, just as in a shipwreck, when we are already overwhelmed on all sides by waves, we try to embrace and hold onto whatever favorably comes our way; so in this tempest of the Republic, we must bend all our effort toward that which opens the way for us to safety and security.

I do not say this because I presume so much of myself that I trust I will fully explain this arduous and complicated matter; but because I have seen others, who have been engaged in this kind of writing, either not sufficiently grasping the matter itself, or being circumscribed by certain narrow limits, failing to traverse fields that lie open wide enough. **Aristotle** indeed, a man of the highest genius and most exact judgment, wrote about the Republic; but he proposed a form that can hardly, or perhaps not at all, be found in any city. **Plato** truly imagines a republic more than he teaches it: and both seem to me to have proposed not so much true Republics, as a certain shadow and image of a Republic. **Machiavelli**, however, who flourished much later, discussed not so much the Republic as the tyrant, and those arts which tyrants are accustomed to use to preserve their power—which arts experience itself has taught us are not only useless, but even destructive. There remained, therefore, others who, even if not as acutely as those men, nevertheless wrote something about this matter; but they likewise either [erred] too much in...

a 2 <note>This "a 2" is a signature mark, used by early modern printers to keep the folded pages of a book in the correct order.</note>

<summary>In this preface, Jean Bodin justifies the necessity of his work by arguing that contemporary states are in a "tempest" of disorder. He critiques his predecessors—Aristotle, Plato, and Machiavelli—for being either too idealistic or too focused on the immoral tactics of tyrants.</summary>
<keywords>Claude de la Guiche, political science, Aristotle, Plato, Machiavelli, Republic, tyranny, French Wars of Religion, sovereignty</keywords>

# PREFACE.

...remained stuck in words, or not being sufficiently skilled in affairs, they did not explain them with enough diligence. But I, when I saw this discipline <note>Referring to political science or the study of the state.</note> lying almost deserted and neglected, could not restrain myself from devoting all my effort and diligence to it: especially since I perceived in our France—once a most flourishing empire—that such great disturbances and upheavals have arisen, that it now seems a struggle not over the **form of the Commonwealth**, but over its very safety and destruction.

For what is there that ought to dismay us more and move us to pity, than when we see our citizens, who ought to worship the same homeland, the same gods, and the same sacred things, rushing into mutual slaughter and internal destruction? When we see cities plundered, temples despoiled, fields laid waste, laws despised, and right and wrong <note>original: "ius fasque," referring to both human law and divine/natural law</note> mixed together in confusion? When I saw these things and reflected upon them, no other way seemed more suitable for settling these discords and restoring peace than if we were brought back to that ancient and best form of the <term>Commonwealth</term> <note>original: "Respublica." While often translated as "Republic," Bodin uses it to mean the state or the "common weal" in general, regardless of whether it is a monarchy or a democracy.</note>: in which indeed the authority of kings, the sanctity of laws, and the harmony of citizens would be at their peak.

Therefore, I undertook this labor on the Commonwealth, not to fashion certain new laws or forms (which would be rash and arrogant), but to collect those which were most wisely established by the ancients—and proven by the longest use and experience—from various monuments of writers, and reduce them into one body. I have sought to confirm them by reasons and examples, so that from here, as if from a mirror, some might be able to look upon what should be followed and what should be avoided in every Commonwealth.

Nor indeed was I ignorant of how envious and dangerous this writing would be, especially at this time when there are so many variations and dissensions of opinion: but nevertheless, love for the homeland and zeal for the common utility prevailed, which impelled me not to refuse this labor.

To you indeed, Most Illustrious Prelate, I wished to dedicate this work, not only on account of your great benevolence toward me, but much more on account of your exceptional prudence and experience in affairs, by which you have shone in governing both ecclesiastical and civil matters. For to you, by whose counsel and authority the Commonwealth has so often been supported, this book on the Commonwealth is deservedly owed: so that you, who sustain the reality itself in deed, may also provide, as it were, a testimony to our writings.

Receive therefore this labor of mine with the spirit in which it is offered: and if there should be any error in it (for it does not escape me how easy it is to slip in such a variety of matters), pardon it by your kindness, and correct it according to your wisdom. Farewell. 

Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ Parisiorum"</note>, June 11, 1586 <note>original: "III. Idus Iunii, M. D. LXXXVI."</note>.

Your Most Reverend Lordship's <note>T.R.D. likely abbreviates "Tuae Reverendissimae Dominationis"</note>
Most studious and devoted client,
**JEAN BODIN.**

# JEAN BODIN'S
# FIRST BOOK. 1

->JEAN BODIN<-
->OF ANGERS,<-
->ON THE COMMONWEALTH<-
->BOOK ONE.<-

## CHAPTER I.
### What the end <note>In this context, "end" refers to the *telos*—the ultimate goal, purpose, or final objective toward which a society strives.</note> of a best-constituted Commonwealth ought to be.

A **COMMONWEALTH** is the rightful government of families and of those things which are common among them, with supreme power. We place this definition first because in all matters, anyone who wishes to follow a correct course of reasoning must keep the end in view. For just as an archer, unless he has a target set before him, shoots his arrows in vain; so too in the organizing of a Commonwealth, one's labor will be wasted unless a certain end is established.

The end of a Commonwealth is defined differently by different people. Indeed, philosophers have disagreed most sharply on this matter: for some have placed the "highest good" in pleasure, others in honesty, some in action, and others in contemplation. But we, setting aside those disputes which do not belong to this place, say that a Commonwealth is rightly established when it is directed toward that end which is proposed for man—which is not one single thing, but a gathering of many things. For a Commonwealth cannot be content with any single thing; rather, many things are required for its preservation and happiness. 

And just as in a human being we must consider not only the body but also the soul, so in a Commonwealth we must seek out not only those things which pertain to physical necessities, but much more those things which contribute to the cultivation of the soul and the splendor of virtue.

A Commonwealth, therefore, is a **rightful government**: by this word, a Commonwealth is distinguished from bands of thieves and pirates. For although such groups may be joined among themselves by a kind of society and hold things in common, they cannot be called a Commonwealth, because they lack justice, and their society tends not toward a legitimate end but toward injury and plunder. **Rightful government**, therefore, is that which is conformable to just laws and the reason of nature. 

Furthermore, this government refers to **families** and to **common things**. For the family is, as it were, the nursery <note>original: "seminarium," meaning a seedbed or a place where young plants are raised before being transplanted.</note> of the Commonwealth: and just as one body is made up of many members, so the Commonwealth exists from many families. By "common things," we mean those which do not belong to any one person privately, but to all together: such as temples, porticos, roads, marketplaces, the treasury, laws, legal judgments, and other things of that kind.

<summary>This page introduces Bodin's famous definition of the Commonwealth, emphasizing that a state must be a "rightful government" governed by justice and supreme power, rather than mere force.</summary>
<keywords>Commonwealth, sovereignty, rightful government, end of the state, family as nursery, common goods, justice vs piracy</keywords>

->POPE CLEMENT VIII<-
->For the future memory of the matter.<- <note>original: "Ad futuram rei memoriam" — a standard opening for papal documents intended to serve as a permanent record.</note>

The Roman Pontiff willingly adds the strength of Apostolic protection to those things which are said to have been providently done for the benefit and utility of persons serving God in the clerical state, so that they may remain undisturbed when such protection is requested of him. Recently, on behalf of our beloved son Domenico of San Ginesio, a clerk of Camerino and a courier <note>A "cursor" was a formal messenger or agent of the papal court.</note> of our Most Holy Lord the Pope, it was explained to us that Pope Innocent IX of pious memory, our predecessor, through certain letters issued in the form of a Brief on the sixteenth day of December last past, had granted certain then-expressed faculties <note>Legal powers or permissions</note> to our beloved son Peter of Lucca, a clerk of Lucca and likewise a courier of the said Most Holy Lord, for the purposes contained in the said letters, as is more fully contained therein. 

Since, however, as the same explanation added, the said Peter has ceded and assigned all and singular such faculties granted to him in the said letters to the same Domenico in their entirety, and has so commanded, as is said to appear through a public instrument <note>A notarized legal document</note> regarding such a transfer. We, considering the aforesaid transfer and mandate, and all and singular things contained in the said letters, as ratified and pleasing, approve and confirm them by Apostolic authority by the tenor of these presents, and decree them to have full strength, correcting any and all defects if any should perhaps have occurred in them. We decree the present letters to be and remain valid and effective, and that they ought to achieve and obtain their full effects. This is notwithstanding Apostolic Constitutions and Ordinances, and all those things which our said predecessor wished not to stand in the way in the aforesaid letters, and any other contrary things whatsoever.

Given at Rome at Saint Peter's, under the Ring of the Fisherman <note>The "Annulus Piscatoris" is the official seal used by the Pope for briefs and private documents.</note>, the 23rd day of July, 1592. In the First Year of Our Pontificate.

M. Vestrius Barbianus. <note>Marcello Vestri Barbiani was a high-ranking papal secretary of the era.</note>

-># POPE PAUL V<-

The sincerity of the exceptional devotion which our beloved sons of the Hermitages and Monasteries of the Congregation of Camaldolese <term>Camaldolese: A branch of the Benedictine order founded by St. Romuald in the 11th century, known for balancing the solitary life of a hermit with communal monasticism.</term> hermit monks of the Order of Saint Benedict bear toward Us and the Apostolic See deserves that We strengthen with Apostolic protection those things which have been providently done by our Predecessors for that Order and its members, for the peace of their souls, and for the fostering and preservation of divine worship everywhere. _Pius, Pope V. For the perpetual memory of the matter. It is consistent with reason and befits honor that those things which have been providently done by us for the increase of divine worship and the peace of persons serving the Lord under the yoke of religion, should remain untouched, and that we add the strength of Apostolic protection to them. Recently, for certain reasonable causes expressed at that time, we separated and exempted the Hermitages and Monasteries of the Holy Angels of Florence and of Saint Benedict of Valdicastro, as well as any other Monasteries and places of the Hermitish Congregation of Camaldolese hermit monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, from any other Monasteries, Hermitages, and the General Chapter and Superiors of the other Camaldolese Congregation, or in any other way whatsoever; and we decreed that they be governed and ruled as one body, and under one regime and the jurisdiction of one General Prior and General Chapter, according to their institutes and constitutions, and we performed other acts, as is more fully contained in our various letters composed regarding this matter._ 

We, therefore, desiring that this separation and exemption, and the other matters contained in the said letters, be observed inviolably for all future times, and that the persons living in the said Hermitages and Monasteries may be able to devote themselves to the Divine more peacefully; for the sake of the Order itself and its preservation, by our own accord <note>original: "Motu proprio" — a document issued by the Pope on his own initiative rather than in response to a request.</note>, and from certain knowledge and our mature deliberation, and from the fullness of the Apostolic power, we approve and confirm by the tenor of these presents all and singular the letters and whatever is contained in them by Apostolic authority, and we decree that they obtain the strength of perpetual stability, making up for all and singular defects, if any should have happened to occur in them. Decreeing that the present letters are and shall be valid and effective, and ought to achieve and obtain their full effects. Notwithstanding Apostolic Constitutions and Orders, and all those things which the said predecessor wished not to stand in the way in the aforesaid letters, and any other contrary things whatsoever.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter's, under the Ring of the Fisherman <note>The personal seal used by the Pope for briefs and private correspondence, depicting St. Peter fishing from a boat.</note>, on the 2nd day of January, 1606. In the First Year of Our Pontificate.

THE affection of sincere devotion, which our beloved sons of the Hermitages and Monasteries of the Camaldolese Congregation of hermit monks of the Order of Saint Benedict <term>Order of Saint Benedict: The parent monastic order of the Camaldolese, following the Rule of St. Benedict but with a specific focus on the hermit life.</term> bear toward Us and the Apostolic See, deserves that we strengthen with Apostolic support those things which were providently done by the Roman Pontiffs, our predecessors, for their peace and convenience. We grant to the same Prior General that he may and can reside and dwell in the said Monastery for the three years of his leadership, and there celebrate the General Chapter of the same Congregation every three years.

By Apostolic authority, through the tenor of these presents, we approve and confirm these letters and everything contained within them, and we decree that they obtain the strength of perpetual stability, supplying any and all defects if any should perhaps have occurred in them. We decree that these present letters are and shall be valid and effective, and ought to sort and obtain their full effects. This is notwithstanding the Apostolic Constitutions and Ordinances, and all those things which the said Clement, our predecessor, willed not to stand in the way in his letters, and any other contraries whatsoever.

Recently, for certain reasonable causes expressed at that time, we separated and exempted the Hermitages and Monasteries of the Holy Angels of Florence, and of Saint Benedict of Valdicastro, as well as other Monasteries and any locations whatsoever of the Eremitic Congregation of Camaldolese monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, from any other Monasteries, Hermitages, and the General Chapter and Superiors of the other Camaldolese Congregation <note>This refers to the "Cenobitic" or community-living branch of the Camaldolese, from which the Monte Corona hermits were being legally separated.</note>, or in any other way whatsoever; and we decreed that they be governed and ruled as one body, and under one government and the jurisdiction of one Prior General and a General Chapter according to their institutes and constitutions, and we performed other acts, as is more fully contained in our various letters composed regarding these matters._

We, therefore, desiring that this separation and exemption, and the other things contained in the said letters, be observed inviolably for all future times, and so that the persons living in the said Hermitages and Monasteries may be able to devote themselves to God more quietly, and for the sake of that Order and its preservation, by our own initiative <term>own initiative: Translates "Motu proprio," a document issued by the Pope personally rather than in response to a request.</term>, and from our certain knowledge and mature deliberation, and from the fullness of the Apostolic power, we approve and confirm by the tenor of these present documents all and individual letters, and whatever is contained in them, by our Apostolic authority. We decree that they obtain the strength of perpetual firmness, making up for all and individual defects, if any should have happened to occur in them. We decree that these present letters are and shall be valid and effective, and ought to sort and obtain their full effects. This is notwithstanding Apostolic Constitutions and Orders, as well as those of Viterbo and other cities and dioceses, and all those things which the said predecessor wished not to stand in the way in the aforementioned letters, and any other contrary things whatsoever.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter's, under the Ring of the Fisherman <term>Ring of the Fisherman: The official signet ring used by the Pope to seal personal or administrative correspondence (briefs) rather than formal bulls.</term>, on the 12th day of May, 1606, in the first year of our Pontificate.

M. Vestrius Barbianus.

<summary>In this 1606 decree, Pope Paul V formally confirms the organizational independence of the Camaldolese Hermits of Monte Corona, upholding a previous separation from the main Camaldolese body granted by Pope Pius V.</summary>

-># TO THE DIVINE CHARLES V,<-
-># EVER AUGUST EMPEROR.<-
->### THE PREFACE OF PAOLO GIOVIO OF COMO TO THE HISTORIES OF HIS OWN TIME.<-

Great Emperor, as I write these <term>commentaries</term> <note>Giovio uses the term "commentarios" in the tradition of Julius Caesar, implying a clear, direct historical record of military and political events</note> of history, in which I recount the events of the last forty years of this century, it often seems to me that my decision to do so was spurred by just and weighty reasons. I was encouraged to complete this work not only by my reverence for your divine praise and virtue, but also by a concern for the common good. My aim is to look after the memory and posterity of kings and peoples, so that I might be seen as one who leaves behind—not from small matters, but from the illustrious events that have shaken our entire world during these years—a magnificent monument to your glory and a collection of examples for future generations.

Therefore, when I noticed that many writers have emerged from various places—some driven by partisan zeal, others (amidst the rough and confused turmoil of events) failing to grasp the truth and seeming more inclined toward favor or hatred than toward historical accuracy—I thought it would not be out of place if I, alone among them all, were to enter this field. My goal is that, amidst such variety and change of affairs, the truth itself (sought with no less skill than it is successfully explained) might be led out from the thickest darkness into the brilliant light of your name.

For no age—I will not say just in our own times, but not even in those most ancient centuries which the Greeks or Romans sought to immortalize in their writings—ever saw so many and such great transformations of affairs. Unless we say it was by some divine plan that you achieved such a vast empire through the midst of these dangers and crises, nothing in human affairs would ever seem to have been more unstable or more perilous. 

Indeed, if we consider the state of our Italy alone, what else will we see it has been during these years but a kind of arena, in which not only our own princes but almost all foreign kings have fought amongst themselves for supreme power? No one can be ignorant of the calamities, the disasters, the destruction of cities, and finally the total upheaval of all things that followed; there is hardly a province, hardly a city, and finally hardly a single house in all of Italy that has not felt some part of this destiny and common ruin.

Yet, amidst such a great movement of affairs and such a violent onset of fate, nothing has seemed more admirable to me than your singular virtue and almost divine success. Relying on these, you not only sustained the attacks of so many enemies, but also eventually brought those same enemies—defeated and conquered—to the terms of peace and to a state of general tranquility. In accomplishing this feat, your mercy and moderation of spirit shone no less brightly than the force of your arms and the wisdom of your counsel. By granting pardon to your conquered enemies and sometimes even restoring their domains and kingdoms more fully than before, you showed that you did not wish so much to expand the borders of your empire as to look after the peace and tranquility of the Christian <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "reipub." (republic), here referring to the collective body of Christian nations under the Emperor's influence</note>.

Since these things were so, I could not allow such magnificent deeds and such illustrious monuments of your virtue to be either suppressed by silence or handed down to posterity by those writers who write for favor rather than for the truth, differently than the events actually occurred. Another factor in my plan was that, since I had devoted myself entirely to the study of literature from my earliest years and nothing has ever been more important to me than to draw true knowledge of affairs from this light of history, it seemed only right that I should begin with this duty. Thus, the lifelong labor I have spent on these studies might be chiefly employed in illustrating your achievements.

In this task, I have tempered my labor so that I neither fail in reporting the truth nor appear excessive in adorning the dignity of real events. My one constant goal has been to ensure that the integrity of history remains intact, and that the order and sequence of events are so connected that from this knowledge, lessons for living rightly and piously may be drawn.

i iij

-># OF HIS OWN TIME BY PAOLO GIOVIO OF COMO.<-

<margin>Year 1494.</margin> It was the one thousand four hundred and ninety-fourth year since the Christian salvation, when, with the arrival of Charles VIII, King of the French, into Italy—and with the various disasters of war soon arising here and there—the affairs of the <term>Christian republic</term> <note>original: "res christianae reipub." Referring to the collective body of Christian nations, or Christendom</note> first began to be shaken. Then indeed, shattered by the most bitter hatreds of certain kings and peoples among themselves, these affairs fell back into that state in which we now find ourselves: a state truly most calamitous and nearly ruined. <margin>Summary of the whole work.</margin> It is my intention to write of the deeds performed during these years—which are nearly fifty—at home and abroad, by land and sea, and to entrust them to the memory of posterity. My goal is that those who lived through these great upheavals may see, from this knowledge of events, what judgment should be made regarding human affairs in either direction. For this age of ours abounds in nothing more than examples of the variety of human affairs; if we were willing to use these examples correctly, we would not be so deeply mired in these miseries.

At that time, there were in Europe these kings and princes who excelled the others either in power or in dignity. <margin>Which kings flourished in Europe at that time.</margin> <margin>Emperor Maximilian.</margin> Emperor Maximilian <note>Maximilian I (1459–1519), who became Holy Roman Emperor in 1493</note>, whose father Frederick III <margin>Frederick III.</margin> had died shortly before, was reigning in Germany. He was a prince truly magnanimous, and one who, if he had flourished with resources and means equal to his imperial authority, could have been the one man most able to look after the interests of the Christian world. He had a son, Philip, Archduke of Austria <margin>Archduke Philip.</margin> <note>Known as Philip the Handsome, father of the future Emperor Charles V</note>, who ruled over the Belgians and Burgundians, and for whom the succession to the Spanish kingdoms—of which we shall soon speak—was shortly to open.

<meta>The previous page concluded a historical overview of the political state of Europe and the "balance of power" in Italy around the year 1500. ->CONSULTATION VIII.<-
->Concerning that which is just regarding those who do not have a just title to the goods they possess.<-

A **just title** <note>original: "Iustus titulus," referring to the legal right or valid grounds upon which one claims ownership of property</note> is required by all laws, both Divine and human, so that one may use goods as one’s own; therefore, whoever does not have a **just title** to the goods they possess is not said to possess them justly, but rather unjustly, and against conscience.
But to understand this matter, it must be known that a **just title** is a valid cause for transferring the ownership <note>original: "dominium," the full legal right to control and dispose of property</note> of a thing from one person to another. Furthermore, such a cause is twofold: one is **natural**, and the other is **civil**.
A **natural cause** is that which, by the very nature of the thing and the **law of nations** <note>original: "iure gentium," the common legal principles accepted by all civilized people</note>, is capable of transferring ownership; such as a gift, a purchase, an exchange, inheritance, and similar means. A **civil cause** is that which is capable of transferring ownership solely by **civil law** and the decree of a Prince; such as **prescription** <note>original: "præscriptio," gaining a legal right through the passage of time</note>, **usucapion** <note>original: "vsucapio," the acquisition of property by long-term possession</note>, the legal seizure of goods, and confiscation.

Secondly, it must be known that a title must be **true**, not merely **plausible** <note>original: "coloratus," literally "colored," meaning a claim that looks valid on the surface but has a hidden defect</note> or **supposed** <note>original: "putatiuus"</note>; for a **plausible title** is one that appears just in appearance, and yet in the truth of the matter is not. For example, if someone buys a thing from a person they believe to be the owner when they are not; or if someone receives a thing as a gift from a person who does not have the power to give it. Such a title is not sufficient for transferring ownership, unless **good faith** <note>original: "bona fides"</note> is present alongside the time period predefined by law for prescription.

Thirdly, it must be known that for a title to be just, it is required to be **without defect** <note>original: "sine vitio"</note>. A title is said to have a defect when, in the contract itself or the cause of acquisition, something is missing from those things required by law; for example, if a contract is made through force, or through unjust fear, or through fraud, or if it is made against a legal prohibition. In such cases, the title is defective and does not transfer ownership, except in cases specifically expressed by the law.

Fourthly, it must be known that whoever does not have a **just title** to the goods they possess is bound to restore them to the true owner as soon as they recognize the defect in the title. For since a just title is lacking, the possession is unjust, and the possessor is said to be acting in **bad faith** <note>original: "malæ fidei"</note>, and cannot keep another's property with a good conscience.

Lastly, it must be known that if someone should possess a thing without a just title through ignorance and in **good faith**, they are excused from sin for as long as that ignorance lasts. However, as soon as they are informed of the defect in the title, they are bound to immediate restitution; because **good faith** does not grant a legal right to the thing, but only excuses one from guilt. Let these points suffice for this Consultation.

<summary>This page defines the legal and moral requirements for "just title" in property ownership, distinguishing between natural and civil ways of acquiring goods. It emphasizes that a title must be true and free of defects like fraud or coercion, and that anyone discovering they lack such a title must restore the property to the rightful owner.</summary>
<keywords>just title, property law, natural law, civil law, good faith, bad faith, restitution, ownership, usucapion, legal ethics</keywords>

--- Page 543 ---
<meta>The previous page discussed the concept of a "just title" (iustus titulus), establishing that legal ownership requires a valid natural or civil cause. This page, Consultation IX, moves to the opposite scenario: the moral and legal obligations of those who possess property in "bad faith," knowing it does not belong to them.</meta>

39
## CONSULTATION IX.
->Concerning that which is just regarding those who possess the property of others in bad faith.<-

Having established what we said in the preceding Consultation, it is easy to judge those who possess the property of others in **bad faith** <note>original: "malæ fide," a legal concept where a person knows they have no right to what they hold</note>. A **bad faith possessor** is defined as one who knows, or ought to know, that the thing they possess does not belong to them, but to another.

Regarding these individuals, it must first be known that a bad faith possessor always **sins mortally** by retaining another's property against the will of the owner. This is because from the moment they know the thing belongs to another, they begin to use it as if it were their own; this is considered **theft** <note>original: "furtum"</note> or **robbery** <note>original: "rapina"</note>, depending on the specific manner of their possession.

Secondly, it must be known that a bad faith possessor is bound to the **restitution** <note>original: "restitutio," the act of returning or making personal restoration for a wrong</note> of the thing itself, as well as all the **fruits** <note>original: "fructuum," referring to profits, produce, or income generated by the property</note> which they received from it, or could have received if they had applied proper diligence. Indeed, they are also bound to restore any damages the owner suffered because they were deprived of their property. The reason for this is that bad faith possession is the root of injustice, which creates an obligation not only toward the object itself but toward everything that comes from it, or ought to have come to the owner.

Thirdly, it must be known that if the property perishes while in the hands of a bad faith possessor, even by **accidental chance** <note>original: "casu fortuito," an event that could not be foreseen or prevented</note>, the possessor is held liable for the value of the item. Since they are in "delay" <note>original: "in mora," a legal term for a failure to perform a duty on time</note> of restoring it, the risk of loss belongs to them. An exception exists if they can prove the thing would have perished just as surely in the hands of the owner had it been restored; in that case, some authorities believe the possessor is freed from paying the value, though others hold the contrary view. It is safer, however, to make restitution.

Fourthly, it must be known that if a bad faith possessor has incurred expenses on another's property, a distinction must be made:
1. If they are **necessary expenses** <note>original: "impensæ necessariæ"</note>, without which the thing would have perished, the possessor may deduct these, because the owner would have had to pay them anyway.
2. If they are **useful expenses** <note>original: "vtiles"</note>, which made the property better, the possessor has no right to claim them back, except insofar as the property was made more valuable.
3. If they are **luxury expenses** <note>original: "voluptuariæ"</note>, which relate only to ornament or decoration, the possessor can in no way claim them, though they may remove them if it can be done without damaging the property.

Fifthly, it must be known that if a bad faith possessor sells another's property, they are held liable for every bit of **profit** <note>original: "lucrum"</note> they received from that sale beyond the actual value of the item. This is because that profit came from another's property, the possession of which was unjust.

Lastly, it must be known that a bad faith possessor can never acquire ownership through **prescription** <note>original: "præscribere," the legal process of gaining ownership through the passage of time</note>. According to the **Canons** <note>original: "Canones," referring to Church/Canon Law</note>, good faith is required both at the beginning and throughout the entire duration of the time period. Therefore, no matter how much time passes, the obligation to restore the property always remains. This concludes this Consultation.

<summary>This page outlines the strict moral and legal requirements for "bad faith" possessors, asserting that they must return not only the stolen property but also all potential profits and damages, with no hope of ever gaining legal ownership through the passage of time.</summary>
<keywords>bad faith, restitution, mala fides, canon law, property rights, theft, moral theology, legal expenses</keywords>

--- Page 544 ---
<meta>The previous page introduced Consultation IX, defining a "bad faith possessor" as someone holding property they know belongs to another. It established that such possession is a mortal sin (equivalent to theft or robbery) and that the possessor is fundamentally obligated to restore the item and its fruits to the rightful owner.</meta>

40
## CONSULTATION IX.

Thirdly, it must be known that if a **bad faith possessor** <note>original: "possessor malæ fidei"</note> has consumed the item, given it away, or in any other way **alienated** it <note>to "alienate" means to transfer ownership to another person through sale or gift</note> so that it cannot be restored, they are bound to restore the price or the appraised value of the thing. Furthermore, if they sold it for a higher price than its actual value, they are bound to restore that entire price, because they gained that profit from property that belonged to another. If, however, they sold it for a lower price, they are nonetheless bound to restore the full value of the item, because they unjustly gave away what was not theirs.

Fourthly, it must be known that if a bad faith possessor loses the property of another, or if the item is destroyed while in their possession—even if this happens through no fault of their own—the loss falls upon the possessor. They are bound to restore the item or its value to the owner; this is because, as previously stated, the risk of the object always remains with the bad faith possessor from the moment they are in **default** <term>mora<gloss>a legal term for a delay in fulfilling an obligation, such as the duty to return property</gloss></term> regarding its restoration.

Fifthly, it must be known that a bad faith possessor is not only bound to restore the **fruits** <note>original: "fructus," referring to profits, crops, or rent generated by the property</note> they actually received, but also those that *could* have been received—specifically those the owner would have gathered had the property been returned to them. This is because the bad faith possessor does not just occupy the thing itself, but also blocks the owner's ability to benefit from it.

Sixthly, it must be known that a bad faith possessor who has incurred expenses on another's property may deduct them if they were **necessary expenses** <note>original: "expensas... necessariæ," costs required to keep the item from rotting or being destroyed</note>. This is because the owner would have had to pay these costs anyway, and the owner should not be enriched at another's expense. If the expenses were **useful** <note>original: "vtiles," improvements that increase value but aren't strictly necessary</note>, the possessor cannot claim them unless the property was actually improved and the owner wishes to keep that improvement; in that case, it is fair that the added value be paid to the possessor. If, however, the expenses were **voluptuary** <term>voluptuariæ<gloss>expenses made for luxury or mere pleasure rather than utility</gloss></term>, the possessor has no right to claim them; they may, however, remove these additions if it can be done without damaging the property.

Seventhly, it must be known that if a bad faith possessor holds many items belonging to others and does not have enough means to satisfy everyone, they must first restore property to those whose claims are more certain and whose loss is greater. In this situation, the priority is not determined by the order of time <note>i.e., "first come, first served"</note>, but by the gravity of the injury.

Eighthly, it must be known that a bad faith possessor is not freed from the debt of restitution even if they have become poor. That obligation always remains in the **root of conscience** <note>original: "in radice conscientiæ," a moral debt that persists even if legal enforcement is impossible</note>, and as soon as they come into a more "fruitful fortune" <note>original: "pinguiorem fortunam," meaning a more prosperous financial state</note>, they are bound to satisfy the debt.

Ninthly, it must be known that if a bad faith possessor dies, the obligation of restoration passes to their heirs. If the heirs know the property belongs to someone else, they are themselves bad faith possessors; if they are unaware, they become **good faith possessors**, who will be discussed in the following Consultation. This concludes the present Consultation.

<summary>This page details the strict financial and moral liabilities of a person holding property in bad faith, including the duty to pay for lost or sold items and the inability to escape debt through poverty. It establishes that bad faith possessors assume all risk for the property and must compensate the owner for lost potential profits.</summary>
<keywords>bad faith, restitution, alienation, necessary expenses, useful expenses, voluptuary expenses, debt of conscience, inheritance of debt, mora</keywords>

## ->CONSULTATION X.<-
### Regarding what is just concerning the restitution to be made by those who possessed the property of another in **good faith**.

Two things must be primarily examined here. First, what it means to possess in **good faith**. Second, what the law is in that case, and what ought to be done.

Regarding the first, a **good faith possessor** <note>original: "possessor bonâ fide"</note> is one who believes the thing is their own and has a **just title** <note>a legal basis for ownership, like a deed or bill of sale</note>—at least a **putative** <gloss>assumed or believed to exist, even if it is legally flawed</gloss> one—or certainly is unaware that it belongs to someone else. For example, if someone buys an item from a person they believed was the owner, when they were not; or if someone receives it through a gift, an inheritance, or a similar title. This good faith must be grounded in a **probable error** <note>a mistake that a reasonable person might make under the circumstances</note>; for if the error were **gross** or **supine** <term>crassus vel supinus<gloss>legal terms for extreme negligence or "blindness" to facts that should be obvious to anyone</gloss></term>, it would not excuse one from bad faith, at least in the **court of conscience** <note>referring to one's moral and spiritual standing before God, rather than just secular law</note>.

Regarding the second, it must first be known that a good faith possessor, as long as they remain in that faith, is not bound to restore the item nor its fruits; indeed, they do not sin by retaining the item, because they believe it to be their own.

Secondly, it must be known that after the possessor learns the item belongs to another, they immediately cease to be a good faith possessor and begin to be a **bad faith possessor**. Consequently, they are then bound to restore the item itself, if it still exists; and if they have consumed it, they are not bound to pay its value, except to the extent that they were made wealthier by it—that is, unless they consumed it for necessary expenses that they would have otherwise had to pay out of their own pocket.

Thirdly, it must be known that a good faith possessor is not bound for the **fruits** <note>original: "fructus," referring to profits, rents, or produce generated by the property</note> they gathered and consumed while existing in good faith; for they are seen to make that profit by their own right until they are informed otherwise regarding another's property. If, however, the fruits still exist, they are bound to restore them to the owner of the item; because fruits follow their owner, and the possessor has no title to them against the true owner.

Fourthly, it must be known that if a good faith possessor sold the property of another before they knew it belonged to another, they are not bound except for what they gained from that sale above the price they paid for it. If they gave it as a gift, they are not bound to restore anything at all, except to the extent that by giving it away, they spared themselves their own expenses which they would have otherwise incurred.

Fifthly, it must be known that if the item perishes while in the hands of the good faith possessor, they are not bound for its value; because the risk of the item belongs to the owner, and the possessor is not seen to be at fault, nor in **default** <term>mora<gloss>a legal term for a delay in fulfilling an obligation, such as the duty to return property</gloss></term>. Let these things be said regarding this Consultation.

<summary>This page defines a "good faith possessor" as someone who honestly believes they own an item through a legitimate but mistaken title, and outlines their limited obligations for restitution compared to those acting in bad faith.</summary>
<keywords>good faith, bona fide, restitution, legal title, probable error, fruits, default, moral theology</keywords>

## ->CONSULTATION XI.<-
### Regarding what is just concerning the restitution to be made by those who have possessed the property of another in **doubtful faith**.

In this Consultation, two things must be considered. First, what **doubtful faith** is. Second, what justice requires in this case.

Regarding the first, **doubtful faith** <note>original: "dubia fides"</note> is that which occurs when the possessor doubts whether a thing belongs to them or to someone else, and has probable reasons for both sides. For example, if someone hears that an item they purchased might have been stolen from the true owner, and they cannot obtain certainty on this matter.

Regarding the second, it must first be known that if the doubt arises at the very beginning of possession, the possessor should not receive or take hold of the thing; for in doubtful matters, the safer path must be chosen. If they do take possession, they are seen to sin and become a **bad faith possessor**.

Second, it must be known that if the doubt arises after possession has already begun in **good faith**, the possessor is not bound to restore the thing immediately. However, they are bound to diligently investigate the truth. If, after such diligence has been applied, they remain in doubt, some believe they may keep the item, because "in a case of doubt, the condition of the possessor is better" <gloss>original: "in dubio melior est conditio possidentis"—a legal principle suggesting that without proof of a superior claim, the current holder has the advantage</gloss>. Others, however, say that the thing should then be divided between the holder and the owner, according to the probability of each one's right; this seems fairer in the **court of conscience** <note>referring to the moral and spiritual judgment of one's soul, as opposed to a civil court of law</note>.

Third, it must be known that if a possessor, while in doubt, neglects to seek the truth, they sin and begin to be a **bad faith possessor**; for it appears they are unwilling to know the truth so that they are not forced to make restitution.

Fourth, it must be known that if the possessor finds nothing certain after a diligent search and remains in doubt, the safest course is to give something in alms, or for the benefit of the soul of the unknown owner, so that they may free their conscience—especially if the item is of significant value.

Fifth, it must be known that a judge in such doubtful cases must always follow the written law; if there is none, they must follow **equity** <note>fairness based on the spirit of the law and natural justice</note>, having regard for the persons and the circumstances of the matter.

Finally, it must be known that if the truth later comes to light and it is established that the thing belongs to another, the possessor who was in doubt is bound to full restitution. This is because doubt does not take away the owner's right, but only excuses the possessor from **formal sin** <gloss>a sin committed with full knowledge and intent</gloss> in the meantime. Let these things be said regarding this Consultation.

<summary>This page explores the ethics of "doubtful faith," where a person is unsure if they rightfully own a piece of property. It outlines the moral obligations to investigate the truth and the eventual necessity of restitution if the true owner is identified.</summary>
<keywords>doubtful faith, restitution, ethics, equity, legal possession, court of conscience, bad faith possessor</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion within Consultation XI regarding the moral obligations of property and justice. While the previous page defined "doubtful faith" in possession, this page shifts to Proposition I, examining the broader relationship between man-made laws (Civil and Canon) and the internal moral obligation of the "forum of conscience."</meta>

### ->PROPOSITION I.<-

Since in the **forum of conscience** <note>original: "foro conscientiae" — the internal "court" of an individual's moral and spiritual responsibility before God, as opposed to a public legal court</note> all laws and statutes, both **Civil** and **Church** <note>original: "Canonica" — referring to Canon Law, the internal legal system of the Catholic Church</note>, are binding with the force of law and carry the weight of sin [if broken], as was proven in Part 1, Title 1, Chapter 4. Insofar as we are dealing here with matters of **Justice**, we conclude from the points made there that both those who do not observe laws and statutes, and those who deliver legal judgments against them, sin against Justice—be it **legal** or **commutative**.

Those who violate or neglect laws sin against **legal justice** <term>Legal justice: the moral obligation of individuals to act in ways that support the "common good" or the well-being of society as a whole</term> because they do not appear to care for the common good which the lawmaker intended to protect. On the other hand, those who withhold, take away, or fail to pay what is owed to another person according to a specific statute or law sin against **commutative justice** <term>Commutative justice: the duty of fairness in private exchanges and contracts, ensuring that each individual receives exactly what is their due</term>. Consequently, such a person is bound to make **restitution**.

2. Furthermore, this must be held as a most certain rule: if statutes or laws are enacted unjustly and against reason, they are in no way to be obeyed, nor do they have the force of law, as they go against **natural law** or **divine law**. The situation is different if the laws are merely very burdensome, unless they are so severe that they are beyond a person's capacity to endure. In such a case, if a tax <note>original: "tributum"</note> or something similar is imposed by a law or statute, one is not required to pay it; likewise, a judge is not required to issue a sentence based upon it.

<summary>This page explores how civil and religious laws create moral obligations in the "forum of conscience," distinguishing between sins against the common good and sins against individuals. It also establishes the principle that laws which contradict natural or divine reason are not morally binding.</summary>
<keywords>forum of conscience, civil law, canon law, legal justice, commutative justice, restitution, unjust laws, natural law, divine law, taxes</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis from Proposition I. While the previous page focused on the "forum of conscience" (the internal moral state), this page moves to Proposition II, which defines the specific requirements for a law to be valid and binding in the "external forum" (the public legal system).</meta>

### ->PROPOSITION II.<-

In the **external forum** <note>original: "foro exteriori" — the public legal system and courts of law, as opposed to the internal "forum of conscience"</note>, however, for decrees and statutes to possess the force of law and to be binding, several conditions are required. The first is the **authority of the lawmaker**. The second is that the law must be **reasonable and honorable**. The third is that it must be **possible to fulfill**. The fourth is that it must be **useful for the common good**. The fifth is that it must be **manifest and clearly written**, as these and other conditions are contained in the legal text *In Istis* (Distinction 4), which we discussed fully in Part 1, Title 1, Chapter 4, from number 7 onwards. To these, we now add another essential condition: **acceptance by the people**.

2. Regarding this condition of **popular acceptance**, there is a great controversy among the Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to "Doctors of the Law"—authoritative legal and theological scholars like Thomas Aquinas or Gratian</note>, which we addressed in the location cited above at number 16. There, we noted that the more common opinion is that popular acceptance is not strictly essential to the nature of human law; rather, once a law has been made by a lawmaker possessing full authority, the people are bound to accept it.

However, the opposite view seems more likely to be true: since the power to create laws belongs to the people by **natural right** <term>Natural right (de jure naturae): a philosophy that certain rights or powers are inherent by virtue of human nature and can be understood universally through human reason</term>—as we stated there in number 13—the people themselves, when transferring that power to a Prince, do not seem to have stripped themselves of the authority to refuse acceptance of laws. This is especially true since the aforementioned legal text *In Istis* expressly states that "laws are instituted when they are promulgated, but they are confirmed when they are approved by the customs of those who use them" <note>original: "leges instituantur cum promulgantur, firmantur autem cum moribus utentium approbantur" — a famous principle from the Decretum Gratiani (Dist. 4, c. 3) suggesting that long-term social practice is necessary to "cement" a law's validity</note>.

<summary>This page outlines the five traditional requirements for a valid law (authority, reason, possibility, utility, and clarity) and debates whether a law must be accepted by the public to be binding. The author favors the view that because legal power originates with the people, their customary approval is necessary to confirm a law's authority.</summary>

<keywords>external forum, legislative authority, common good, popular acceptance, natural right, legal validity, customs, Prince’s power</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the general requirements of a valid law (Proposition II) to the legal presumption of a law’s validity and its moral consequences (Proposition III). It continues the discussion on how laws bind an individual both in their private conscience and in public society.</meta>

### ->PROPOSITION III.<-

In cases of doubt, laws and statutes are to be presumed just, pious, reasonable, and useful, both in the **court of conscience** <note>original: "forum conscientiae" — the internal realm of moral responsibility and one's relationship with God</note> and in the **external court** <note>original: "forum exteriori" — the public legal system and human courts</note>, unless the contrary is clearly manifest, or it is evident that the lawmaker lacked sufficient authority. This is not the appropriate place to argue about that authority, nor to discuss the specific nature of church (canonical) or papal statutes. Instead, it must be held as a rule here that statutes and laws are to be observed in both the internal court of conscience and the external legal court. Furthermore, they create an obligation for **restitution** <term>Restitution (restitutio): the moral and legal requirement to restore what has been taken or to repair a harm caused by an act of injustice</term> if their violation leads to an act against justice.

2. From this, it is first inferred that a statute or a custom that commands an action resulting in harm to another person—if that harm is unjust—is certainly not to be followed. For example, a rule stating that beggars should not be received, or that a person should be driven out of their own home to give it to others, is not to be obeyed unless there is a great and urgent necessity for the **republic** <note>original: "reipublicae" — the state or the common good of the community</note>.

3. Secondly, it is inferred that a statute commanding the condemnation of an innocent person, or the acquittal of a guilty one, is in no way valid. Even though the law might say a judge must rule **according to what is alleged and proven** <note>original: "secundùm allegata & probata" — a legal principle meaning a judge should only consider evidence officially presented in court</note>, even if this contradicts the truth known to the judge privately, several **Doctors** <note>Scholarly authorities in law and theology</note> argue about this in various ways (as we discussed in Part 1, Title 4, Chapter 1, numbers 16 and 17). But here I say that in such a case, one must place more faith in the **truth** than in the written legal record. Thus, a judge ought to acquit the innocent even if there is evidence against them, and condemn the guilty even if no evidence is produced against them.

<summary>This page argues that laws should be presumed just and binding unless they clearly cause injustice, specifically addressing the moral dilemma of a judge who knows the truth but faces conflicting legal evidence.</summary>
<keywords>legal presumption, court of conscience, external forum, restitution, common good, judicial ethics, evidence vs. truth</keywords>
