### THE HISTORY OF GAUL, BOOK I. 707

<margin>The Hercynian Forest.</margin> The **Hercynian Forest** <note>A vast, ancient forest region in Central Europe, located east of the Rhine</note>, which is beyond the Rhine and extends into Germany, sent forth the Gauls when the borders of Gaul became too narrow to contain their great numbers. Therefore, **Ambigatus**, King of the **Bituriges** <note>A powerful Celtic tribe in central Gaul, centered on modern-day Bourges</note>, who then held supreme power in Gaul, sent the sons of his sister— <margin>Segovesus.</margin> **Segovesus** and <margin>Bellovesus.</margin> **Bellovesus**—into different parts of the world. Segovesus departed for the Hercynian Forest. Bellovesus, however, having gathered a great multitude of Gauls—including the Bituriges, Arverni, Senones, Haedui, Ambarri, Carnutes, and Aulerci—came into Italy. <margin>The Insubrian Gauls.</margin> And when he had reached the **Taurine Pass** <note>The mountain passes near modern Turin</note>, finding there the **Insubrian Gauls** (who themselves had also arrived from Gaul), he gave them land to cultivate. <margin>The Cenomanni Gauls.</margin> The **Cenomanni Gauls**, under the leadership of **Elitovius**, arrived in Italy at nearly the same time and occupied the places we now call **Brescia** and **Verona**. <margin>The Libui Gauls.</margin> After these came the **Libui** and the <margin>The Saluvii Gauls.</margin> **Saluvii**, who settled in the lands around the river **Ticino**. <margin>The Boii Gauls.</margin> Then the **Boii** and the <margin>The Lingonian Gauls.</margin> **Lingones** crossed over the **Po** <note>The largest river in Italy; Latin: *Padus*</note> and occupied the regions located between the Po and the Apennine Mountains. <margin>The Senonian Gauls.</margin> Finally, the **Senonian Gauls** arrived and extended their borders as far as the territory of the **Umbrians**. These were the ones who burned the City of Rome. <margin>The Gauls conquered by Marcellus.</margin> However, the Insubrian Gauls, after they were defeated by **Marcus Marcellus**, fell under the dominion of the Romans. <margin>The Gauls conquered by Scipio.</margin> Later, they were completely subdued by **Scipio Nasica** and the consul **Gaius Cornelius**.

<summary>This page describes the primary migrations of Gallic tribes into Northern Italy (Cisalpine Gaul) and Germany, naming the specific tribes and their eventual defeat by Roman generals.</summary>

708 ANDREA ALCIATI

<margin>The origin of Milan.</margin> **Milan** <note>Latin: *Mediolanum*</note> was founded by the **Insubrian Gauls**, as **Cato** <note>Marcus Porcius Cato, known as Cato the Elder (234–149 BC), whose lost work *Origines* dealt with the history of Italian cities</note> writes in his *Origins*. But it was fortified and enlarged by **King Bellovesus**, <margin>How Milan was named.</margin> as **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian who chronicled the Gallic migration in his *History of Rome*</note> maintains. It received its name, however, from a <margin>The woolly sow.</margin> **woolly sow** found there, which was woolly in the middle of its body, as **Sidonius Apollinaris** <note>A 5th-century poet and bishop; the name *Medio-lanum* was traditionally explained as a compound of "middle" (*medio*) and "wool" (*lana*)</note> writes. 

Although others think the city was named after a certain **Mediolanus**, a leader of the Gauls. <margin>Milan, the metropolis of Insubria.</margin> Milan is the head of **Insubria** and the metropolis of the region contained between the **Po**, the **Ticino**, the **Adda**, and the **Alps**. They call this region Insubria after the Insubrian Gauls, who were the first to inhabit it. <margin>The Gauls defeated by Marcellus.</margin> These people were first defeated by **Marcus Claudius Marcellus** <note>The Roman general who won the *spolia opima* by killing the Insubrian king Viridomarus in 222 BC</note>. <margin>The Gauls defeated by Scipio.</margin> They were later defeated by **Scipio Nasica** and the consul **Gaius Cornelius**, at which time it is said that fifteen thousand Gauls were killed. Finally, having been thoroughly conquered by **Cornelius Scipio**, they were brought under the dominion of the Romans.
